ILO: Analyze ethical dilemmas in project scenarios, applying professional codes of conduct to propose responsible solutions.
TC: Ethical Dilemma Analysis & Professional Conduct Application- Step 1: Case Study Review. Present groups with real-world project scenarios involving ethical conflicts (e.g., data privacy breaches, resource allocation fairness, stakeholder misrepresentation). Groups identify 2-3 key ethical issues using a "Dilemma Framework" (e.g., conflict of interest, transparency gaps, accountability lapses).- Step 2: Code of Conduct Application. For each issue, groups reference relevant professional standards (e.g., IEEE ethics for engineering, APA guidelines for social sciences) to draft: 1) Ethical resolution steps (e.g., "Implement anonymized data protocols"), 2) Preventive policies (e.g., "Establish clear consent forms for stakeholder interviews"), 3) Documentation for accountability (e.g., "Maintain an ethics log in project Feishu").

ILO: Develop transparent communication protocols to ensure stakeholder trust and project integrity, addressing confidentiality and honesty in reporting.
TC: Transparent Communication & Stakeholder Trust Building- Key strategies for Rubric 2.1 (Professional Communication):1. Design communication plans: Outline regular updates (e.g., bi-weekly reports) using clear, jargon-free language accessible to all stakeholders.2. Avoid common pitfalls: Withholding negative results, overpromising outcomes, or using ambiguous metrics.- Key strategies for Rubric 2.2 (Integrity in Reporting):1. Implement honesty protocols: Document all data sources and limitations openly (e.g., "Section 3.1: Data Collection Methods & Potential Biases").2. Ensure confidentiality: Use secure channels for sensitive information and obtain explicit permissions for sharing (e.g., "Encrypt stakeholder feedback in cloud storage").

ILO: Evaluate project decisions for social and environmental impact, aligning outcomes with sustainable and equitable principles.Transferable Skills: Ethical Reasoning, Impact Assessment (Social-Environmental Responsibility)
TC: Prompt groups to assess their project's broader effects using an "Impact Matrix" (social × environmental dimensions).Discuss how to integrate responsibility: For example, an engineering solution's carbon footprint analysis or a sociology study's community equity considerations.Draft 1-2 action items per group linking decisions to responsible outcomes (e.g., "Our design minimizes e-waste by using modular components, supporting environmental sustainability").

ILO: Analyze building design scenarios to identify applicable health and safety codes, regulations, and architectural standards that protect public welfare. Transferable Skills: Regulatory Analysis, Critical Thinking in Design Contexts
TC: Health & Safety Code Application Framework- Step 1: Scenario Analysis. Present real-world building design scenarios (e.g., multi-use commercial/residential complex, educational facility). Guide students to identify key health/safety risks (e.g., fire hazards, accessibility barriers, structural integrity).- Step 2: Regulatory Mapping. Teach how to map risks to specific codes/standards: a. International Building Code (IBC) sections for egress and occupancy loads. b. ADA Standards for accessible design requirements. c. Local fire safety regulations for material flammability and alarm systems. Students practice creating a "code compliance matrix" linking design elements to applicable regulations.

ILO: Evaluate architectural and interior design proposals against established health/safety standards to ensure public protection compliance. Transferable Skills: Compliance Auditing, Standards-Based Assessment
TC: Design Proposal Compliance Evaluation- Step 1: Standards-Based Review Protocol. Introduce a structured evaluation template covering: a. Life safety systems (fire suppression, emergency lighting). b. Accessibility features (door widths, ramp gradients, restroom layouts). c. Environmental health factors (ventilation rates, material toxicity).- Step 2: Gap Identification & Documentation. Guide students to review sample design proposals, identify compliance gaps using the template, and document specific code violations with references (e.g., "Section 1005.3.1 IBC requires minimum 44-inch corridor width, proposed design shows 42 inches"). Teams practice creating compliance assessment reports with prioritized recommendations.

ILO: Synthesize multiple regulatory frameworks to develop integrated design solutions that proactively address public health and safety requirements. Transferable Skills: Regulatory Integration, Proactive Design Thinking
TC: Integrated Regulatory Synthesis for Design Solutions- Step 1: Framework Integration. Teach how to reconcile overlapping/conflicting requirements from: a. Building codes (IBC, NFPA). b. Accessibility standards (ADA, ANSI A117.1). c. Sustainability certifications (LEED, WELL Building Standard).- Step 2: Solution Development. Guide students through case studies where they must: a. Create design modifications that satisfy multiple regulatory domains simultaneously (e.g., designing an accessible egress route that also meets fire separation requirements). b. Develop compliance justification documents explaining how the integrated solution meets all applicable standards. Students practice presenting their synthesized solutions with cross-referenced regulatory support.

ILO: Design and facilitate structured peer feedback sessions using established rubrics to guide peers toward excellence in project execution.
TC: - Step 1: Peer Feedback Framework Development. Introduce a structured "Peer Mentoring Framework" with components: 1) Rubric-Based Assessment (using project-specific criteria), 2) Constructive Feedback Guidelines (specific, actionable, supportive), 3) Goal-Setting for Improvement (SMART goals aligned with feedback). - Step 2: Guided Peer Feedback Sessions. Students practice facilitating feedback sessions: a. Prepare by reviewing peer work against rubric criteria to identify strengths and areas for growth. b. Conduct sessions using the "Feedback Sandwich" method (positive → constructive → positive). c. Collaborate with peers to develop actionable improvement plans with clear next steps. Instructor observes and provides guidance on effective mentoring techniques.

ILO: Develop personalized coaching strategies to support peers in overcoming specific project challenges and achieving disciplinary excellence.
TC: Coaching Strategy Development & Implementation - Step 1: Challenge Identification & Strategy Mapping. Guide students to analyze peer project challenges (e.g., technical hurdles, time management issues, research gaps) and map them to appropriate coaching strategies: 1) Technical Mentoring (hands-on guidance), 2) Process Coaching (workflow optimization), 3) Motivational Support (goal reinforcement). - Step 2: Personalized Coaching Plan Creation. Students develop tailored coaching plans for assigned peers: a. Identify 2-3 key areas for improvement based on project progress. b. Design specific coaching interventions (e.g., weekly check-ins, skill-building exercises, resource recommendations). c. Establish success metrics to track peer progress. Instructor reviews plans for appropriateness and effectiveness.

ILO: Create and implement peer support systems that foster collaborative excellence through shared resources, knowledge exchange, and mutual accountability.
TC: - Step 1: Peer Support System Design. Introduce components of effective peer support systems: 1) Knowledge Sharing Platforms (e.g., shared documentation, skill workshops), 2) Accountability Partnerships (paired check-ins, progress tracking), 3) Resource Pool Development (curated materials, tool recommendations). - Step 2: Support System Implementation & Monitoring. Groups establish and test peer support systems: a. Set up regular peer mentoring sessions with clear agendas and objectives. b. Create shared repositories for best practices, troubleshooting guides, and success stories. c. Implement peer accountability mechanisms (e.g., progress dashboards, milestone celebrations). Instructor facilitates reflection on system effectiveness and iterative improvements.

ILO: Recognize and describe key components, relationships, and feedback loops within a complex system to understand its structure and dynamics. Transferable Skills: Systems Thinking (Component Identification), Analytical Observation
TC: System Components & Relationship Mapping- Step 1: System Deconstruction. Guide students to break down a complex system (e.g., urban transportation network) into core components: actors (commuters, operators), resources (vehicles, infrastructure), processes (scheduling, maintenance), and external factors (weather, policies).- Step 2: Relationship Visualization. Teach techniques to map relationships between components using diagrams (e.g., causal loop diagrams, flow charts). Focus on identifying feedback loops (reinforcing/balancing) and interdependencies (e.g., "Increased ridership → more revenue → improved service → further ridership increase").- Step 3: Practice Application. Groups analyze a case study (e.g., a local public transit system), document components and relationships in a shared digital whiteboard, and present their system description highlighting key feedback mechanisms.

ILO: Predict system behavior under different conditions by modeling scenarios and assessing potential outcomes based on identified relationships and feedback loops. Transferable Skills: Scenario Planning, Predictive Analysis
TC: Scenario Modeling & Behavior Prediction- Step 1: Scenario Development. Instruct students to define 2-3 plausible scenarios for a given system (e.g., an e-commerce supply chain) by varying key inputs: a) Baseline (current conditions), b) Disruption (e.g., supplier delay), c) Innovation (e.g., new technology adoption).- Step 2: Behavior Modeling. Guide groups to use simple quantitative or qualitative models (e.g., stock-and-flow diagrams, if-then logic chains) to simulate how the system might respond in each scenario. Emphasize tracing impacts through relationships (e.g., "If supplier delay occurs, then inventory drops → orders backlog → customer satisfaction declines").- Step 3: Outcome Assessment. Students compare predicted outcomes across scenarios, identify tipping points or thresholds (e.g., "Inventory below 10% causes system collapse"), and document uncertainties in their predictions.

ILO: Analyze system behavior to evaluate performance, identify root causes of issues, and propose targeted interventions that leverage system dynamics. Transferable Skills: Root Cause Analysis, Strategic Intervention Design
TC: System Performance Analysis & Intervention Design- Step 1: Performance Metrics & Data Review. Teach students to select relevant metrics (e.g., efficiency, resilience, equity) for a system (e.g., a community recycling program) and review provided data (e.g., participation rates, contamination levels, cost reports).- Step 2: Root Cause Investigation. Guide groups to analyze behavior patterns (e.g., "Why does contamination spike in certain neighborhoods?") using tools like the 5 Whys or fishbone diagrams. Focus on tracing issues back to systemic factors (e.g., feedback loops like "low education → high contamination → reduced funding → fewer education efforts").- Step 3: Intervention Proposal. Students co-develop 1-2 targeted interventions (e.g., "Implement a feedback loop: use contamination data to trigger personalized education campaigns") that address root causes by modifying system components or relationships. Emphasize feasibility and alignment with system dynamics.

ILO: Understand the impact of body language and presence in professional settings, and apply open gestures and movement to project confidence and build rapport with an audience. Transferable Skills: Non-verbal Communication, Presence
TC: Introduction to Body Language & Presence - Discuss the importance of non-verbal communication in professional settings. - Demonstrate and practice open gestures and confident movements. - Conduct a role-play activity where students present a short speech, focusing on using open gestures and confident posture.

ILO: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of different body language techniques in various scenarios, and adapt them to suit the context and audience. Transferable Skills: Contextual Adaptation, Critical Thinking
TC: Analyzing and Adapting Body Language - Provide case studies of different professional scenarios (e.g., job interviews, presentations, networking events). - Have students analyze the body language used in each scenario and discuss its effectiveness. - Practice adapting body language for different contexts, such as formal vs. informal settings, and receive peer feedback.

ILO: Develop and deliver a presentation that effectively uses body language and presence to engage and persuade the audience. Transferable Skills: Presentation Skills, Audience Engagement
TC: Presentation Development and Delivery - Guide students through the process of creating a presentation, emphasizing the use of body language and presence. - Have students prepare and deliver a 5-minute presentation, incorporating open gestures, confident movement, and eye contact. - Provide constructive feedback on the use of body language and presence, and discuss how it can be further improved.

ILO: Craft a compelling narrative that structures project information into a coherent and engaging story, using storytelling techniques to connect with the audience and convey the project's significance.
TC: Narrative Storytelling Workshop:1. Introduction to storytelling elements (e.g., plot, character, setting, conflict, resolution).2. Techniques for structuring a narrative (e.g., the hero’s journey, problem-solution structure).3. Case studies of effective project narratives (e.g., successful pitches, case studies).4. Hands-on practice: Students create a narrative for their project, incorporating key elements and techniques.

ILO: Develop a clear and structured narrative that communicates the project's purpose, process, and impact, using storytelling to make the information more relatable and memorable.
TC: Storytelling for Project Communication:1. Identifying the key messages and themes of the project.2. Structuring the narrative to highlight the project’s purpose, process, and impact.3. Using anecdotes and examples to illustrate key points.4. Peer review and feedback session: Students present their narratives and receive feedback on clarity, engagement, and effectiveness.

ILO: Apply storytelling techniques to create a persuasive and engaging presentation that effectively communicates the project’s value and impact to diverse stakeholders.
TC: Persuasive Storytelling in Presentations:1. Understanding the audience and tailoring the narrative to their needs and interests.2. Techniques for creating a strong opening and closing (e.g., hook, call to action).3. Visual storytelling: Using images, videos, and other visual aids to enhance the narrative.4. Practice and refinement: Students prepare and deliver a short presentation, incorporating storytelling techniques, and receive constructive feedback from peers and instructors.

ILO: Design visually appealing and professional slides that effectively support the main points of a presentation, enhancing the audience's understanding and engagement.
TC: Visual Design for Presentations- Key strategies:1. Use a clean, consistent layout with a clear hierarchy of information.2. Choose appropriate, high-quality images and graphics that complement the content.3. Employ a limited color palette to maintain a professional look.4. Use legible fonts and appropriate font sizes to ensure readability.5. Minimize text and use bullet points or short phrases to convey key messages.

ILO: Create a cohesive and well-structured slide deck that aligns with the flow of the presentation, ensuring that each slide contributes to the overall narrative and supports the speaker's message.
TC: Cohesive Slide Deck Creation- Key strategies:1. Start with an outline or storyboard to plan the structure of the presentation.2. Use a consistent design theme throughout the slide deck.3. Ensure smooth transitions between slides to maintain the flow of the presentation.4. Use visual elements (e.g., charts, diagrams) to illustrate complex ideas.5. Include a summary slide at the end to reinforce the main takeaways.6. Practice the presentation with the slides to ensure timing and alignment.

ILO: Apply best practices in visual design to avoid common pitfalls that can distract from the presentation, such as cluttered slides, excessive text, and poor image quality.
TC: Avoiding Common Visual Design Pitfalls- Key strategies:1. Avoid overcrowding slides with too much text or images.2. Use high-resolution images and avoid pixelated or low-quality visuals.3. Maintain a balance between text and white space to prevent visual overload.4. Use animations and transitions sparingly and purposefully.5. Ensure all visual elements are relevant and add value to the presentation.6. Conduct a peer review to get feedback on the visual design and make necessary adjustments.

ILO: Analyze and understand the specific needs, expertise, and background of a target audience to tailor the tone, depth, and vocabulary of a presentation.
TC: Audience Analysis Techniques- Step 1: Identifying Audience Characteristics (20 mins)Students will brainstorm and list key characteristics of their target audience, such as age, profession, educational background, and prior knowledge.- Step 2: Tailoring Communication (15 mins)Students will practice adjusting the tone, depth, and vocabulary of a sample presentation based on the identified audience characteristics.

ILO: Evaluate and refine a group presentation to ensure it is appropriately tailored to the specific needs and expertise of the intended audience.
TC: Presentation Refinement for Audience- Step 1: Group Presentation Review (20 mins)Teams will present their draft presentations, focusing on the content, tone, and vocabulary used.- Step 2: Peer Feedback and Adjustment (15 mins)Other teams will provide feedback on how well the presentation aligns with the target audience. Teams will then revise their presentations based on the feedback.

ILO: Develop a strategy for adapting a presentation in real-time based on audience reactions and feedback during the delivery.
TC: Real-Time Adaptation Strategies- Step 1: Simulation of Real-Time Feedback (20 mins)Students will deliver a segment of their presentation while the instructor and peers simulate different types of audience reactions (e.g., confusion, boredom, engagement).- Step 2: Debrief and Strategy Development (15 mins)After the simulation, students will discuss what they observed and develop strategies for adapting their presentation in real-time, such as adjusting pace, simplifying complex points, or adding more engaging elements.

ILO: Design and create a visually engaging presentation using boards, slides, or props to effectively communicate the refined problem statement and its significance. Transferable Skills: Use of Instructional Aids (sub-skill: visual communication)
TC: Introduce the principles of effective visual communication. Provide examples of well-designed presentations and discuss what makes them effective. Guide students through the process of creating a visually engaging presentation that includes the refined problem statement, its significance, and key visuals to support their message. Each team will present their work, and peers will provide feedback on the clarity and effectiveness of the visual aids used.

ILO: Develop a storyboard for a short video or animation that explains the refined problem statement and its interdisciplinary potential. Transferable Skills: Use of Instructional Aids (sub-skill: multimedia creation)
TC: Teach the basics of creating a storyboard for a short video or animation. Discuss the importance of storyboarding in ensuring a coherent and engaging narrative. Have each team develop a storyboard that outlines the key points of their refined problem statement and its interdisciplinary potential. Students will then create a rough draft of the video or animation based on the storyboard and present it to the class for feedback.

ILO: Create an interactive infographic that visually represents the problem, its significance, and the proposed solution. Transferable Skills: Use of Instructional Aids (sub-skill: data visualization)
TC: Explain the concept of infographics and their role in data visualization. Provide examples of effective infographics and discuss the elements that make them successful. Instruct students to design an interactive infographic that visually represents the problem, its significance, and the proposed solution. Teams will use tools like Canva, Piktochart, or Adobe Illustrator to create their infographics. The final products will be shared with the class for peer review and feedback.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to modulate pitch, pace, and volume effectively in a 5-minute presentation to maintain audience interest and emphasize key points.
TC: Presentation Practice: Modulating Vocal Variety - Students will practice a 5-minute segment of their project presentation, focusing on varying their pitch, pace, and volume. They will receive feedback from peers and the instructor on how well they maintained interest and emphasized key points. The session will include: 1. A 5-minute presentation by each student, 2. 3 minutes of peer feedback, and 3. 2 minutes of instructor feedback.

ILO: Apply vocal variety techniques to enhance the clarity and impact of a 3-minute peer feedback session, ensuring that the feedback is both constructive and engaging.
TC: Peer Feedback Session: Enhancing Clarity and Impact - Students will provide 3-minute feedback sessions to their peers, using vocal variety to make their feedback more engaging and clear. The session will include: 1. A 3-minute feedback session by each student, 2. 2 minutes of peer feedback on the use of vocal variety, and 3. 1 minute of instructor feedback on the effectiveness of the feedback delivery.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of vocal variety in a 2-minute instructor feedback session, providing specific examples of how pitch, pace, and volume were used to convey key messages and maintain engagement.
TC: Instructor Feedback Session: Evaluating Vocal Variety - The instructor will provide 2-minute feedback sessions to students, demonstrating the use of vocal variety. Students will then evaluate the effectiveness of the instructor's use of pitch, pace, and volume. The session will include: 1. A 2-minute feedback session by the instructor, 2. 2 minutes of student evaluation, and 3. 1 minute of group discussion to share insights and observations.

ILO: Engage in active and collaborative problem-solving to refine project goals and objectives
TC: Collaborative Problem-Solving Session: 1. Divide students into small groups and provide them with a real-world challenge related to the project. 2. Each group brainstorms and identifies key issues, setting clear and measurable project goals. 3. Groups present their refined goals and objectives to the class. 4. Peer feedback session: Students provide constructive feedback on each other's goals, focusing on clarity, measurability, and alignment with the project’s overall objectives. 5. Instructor feedback: Provide guidance on how to further refine and align the goals with the project rubric.

ILO: Apply critical thinking skills to evaluate and improve project proposals
TC: Critical Thinking Workshop: 1. Present a case study or example of a poorly defined project proposal. 2. Students work in pairs to identify the weaknesses in the proposal (e.g., lack of SMART objectives, unclear problem statement). 3. Each pair presents their findings to the class, highlighting specific areas for improvement. 4. Instructor-led discussion: Analyze the common pitfalls and best practices in writing effective project proposals. 5. Individual Reflection: Students reflect on their own project proposals and write a brief summary of improvements they can make.

ILO: Use reflective practice to enhance personal and team learning and development
TC: Reflective Practice Session: 1. Introduce the concept of reflective practice and its importance in project-based learning. 2. Students individually complete a reflective journal entry, focusing on their recent experiences and learning from the project. 3. Small group discussions: Share and discuss the reflections, identifying common themes and insights. 4. Group Action Plan: Based on the reflections, each group develops an action plan to address any identified areas for improvement. 5. Instructor feedback: Provide feedback on the action plans, offering suggestions for implementation and follow-up.

ILO: Provide immediate, constructive feedback to peers on their project proposals using a structured feedback rubric, focusing on clarity, feasibility, and alignment with project goals.
TC: Structured Peer Feedback Session: 1. Introduce the feedback rubric, which includes criteria such as clarity, feasibility, and alignment with project goals. 2. Each student presents their project proposal for 5 minutes. 3. Peers provide immediate, constructive feedback using the rubric, highlighting specific areas for improvement. 4. The instructor facilitates a 10-minute discussion to ensure the feedback is clear and actionable.

ILO: Evaluate and refine project plans based on feedback from instructors and peers, ensuring that the revised plan addresses identified gaps and aligns with project objectives.
TC: Project Plan Refinement Workshop: 1. Students present their initial project plans, focusing on key components such as scope, timeline, and resource allocation. 2. Instructors and peers provide detailed feedback, identifying gaps and suggesting improvements. 3. Students revise their project plans in real-time, incorporating the feedback. 4. The revised plans are shared and discussed in a group setting to ensure they meet the project's objectives.

ILO: Use formative assessment techniques to monitor and provide ongoing feedback to team members during project sprints, ensuring continuous improvement and alignment with project goals.
TC: Formative Assessment and Continuous Feedback: 1. Introduce formative assessment techniques, such as checklists and progress tracking tools. 2. During each sprint, team members use these tools to monitor their progress and provide ongoing feedback to one another. 3. Conduct a mid-sprint review where each team member shares their progress and receives feedback from the team and instructor. 4. Use the feedback to make necessary adjustments to the project plan and ensure continuous improvement.

ILO: Develop a clear and concise project proposal that effectively communicates the project's objectives, scope, and expected outcomes using simple and precise language.
TC: Project Proposal Development- Students will draft their project proposals, focusing on clarity and precision in language. - Instructors will provide examples of well-written and poorly written proposals to highlight the importance of clarity. - Students will receive feedback on their drafts, with a focus on improving the clarity and simplicity of their explanations.

ILO: Explain the key components of the project (e.g., objectives, methodology, timeline) using relevant and relatable examples to ensure understanding by all team members.
TC: Key Components Explanation- Students will prepare a presentation on the key components of their project, using relevant examples to illustrate each point. - Instructors will model how to use simple, precise language and relevant examples to explain complex concepts. - Peer feedback sessions will be conducted to ensure that the explanations are clear and understandable to all team members.

ILO: Revise and refine the project documentation based on peer and instructor feedback, ensuring that the final document is clear, precise, and free of jargon.
TC: Documentation Revision- Students will present their project documentation (e.g., proposal, plan, reports) to the class. - Peers and instructors will provide feedback on the clarity and precision of the language used. - Students will revise their documents based on the feedback, with a focus on eliminating jargon and simplifying complex terms. - A final review session will be held to ensure that the revised documents meet the clarity and precision standards.

ILO: Develop and use open-ended and probing questions to stimulate critical thinking and deeper understanding of the problem statement.Transferable Skills: Questioning Techniques, Critical Thinking
TC: Introduction to Open-Ended and Probing Questions: Explain the importance of using open-ended and probing questions in problem-solving. Provide examples of effective and ineffective questions. Practice Formulating Questions: Students will practice formulating open-ended and probing questions based on a given problem statement. Peer Feedback: Students will share their questions with peers and receive feedback on how to improve them for better critical thinking.

ILO: Apply questioning techniques to guide group discussions and ensure all members contribute to the problem-solving process.Transferable Skills: Questioning Techniques, Facilitation, Teamwork
TC: Facilitating Group Discussions: Discuss the role of a facilitator in guiding group discussions. Teach students how to use questioning techniques to encourage participation from all group members. Role-Playing Activity: Students will take turns acting as the facilitator in a group discussion, using open-ended and probing questions to guide the conversation. Debrief and Reflect: After the activity, students will reflect on the effectiveness of their questioning techniques and discuss how they can improve their facilitation skills.

ILO: Use questioning techniques to challenge assumptions and explore multiple perspectives, leading to more innovative and comprehensive solutions.Transferable Skills: Questioning Techniques, Critical Thinking, Creativity
TC: Challenging Assumptions: Introduce the concept of challenging assumptions in problem-solving. Provide examples of common assumptions that may limit creative solutions. Exploring Multiple Perspectives: Guide students through an exercise where they use questioning techniques to explore different perspectives on a given problem. Encourage them to consider diverse viewpoints and potential solutions. Group Discussion and Reflection: Students will discuss the insights gained from exploring multiple perspectives and reflect on how questioning techniques can lead to more innovative and comprehensive solutions.

ILO: Develop and deliver a clear, concise, and persuasive speech that effectively communicates a message to an audience, using appropriate rhetorical techniques and avoiding filler words. Transferable Skills: Public Speaking, Rhetoric
TC: Teach the fundamentals of public speaking: 1) Structuring a speech (introduction, body, conclusion). 2) Using rhetorical devices (analogies, repetition, rhetorical questions). 3) Managing filler words by practicing pauses and breathing techniques. Provide students with a template for a 5-minute speech on a topic of their choice. Have them practice in small groups, giving and receiving feedback on clarity, persuasiveness, and use of rhetorical techniques.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to engage and maintain the audience's attention through effective use of vocal variety, pacing, and non-verbal communication. Transferable Skills: Public Speaking, Non-Verbal Communication
TC: Instruct students on the importance of vocal variety and non-verbal communication: 1) Varying pitch, tone, and volume to convey emotion and emphasis. 2) Using pauses for dramatic effect and to allow the audience to process information. 3) Utilizing gestures, facial expressions, and eye contact to enhance the message. Conduct a workshop where students practice delivering a 3-minute impromptu speech, focusing on these elements. Use video recordings to help students analyze and improve their delivery.

ILO: Critically evaluate and provide constructive feedback on peers' public speaking performances, focusing on clarity, engagement, and the effective use of rhetorical techniques. Transferable Skills: Critical Evaluation, Peer Feedback
TC: Provide a structured feedback framework: 1) Clarity: Was the message clear and easy to understand? 2) Engagement: Did the speaker maintain the audience's interest? 3) Rhetorical Techniques: Were rhetorical devices used effectively? Organize a peer evaluation session where each student delivers a 5-minute prepared speech. After each speech, have the audience use the feedback framework to provide constructive comments. Facilitate a discussion on common strengths and areas for improvement, and share tips for continuous improvement.

ILO: Design a lesson plan that effectively hooks learners' interest within the first 60 seconds by using engaging and relevant content.
TC: Lesson Plan Design for Engagement- Step 1: Introduction to Hook Techniques. Discuss various techniques to capture students' attention (e.g., storytelling, surprising facts, interactive activities).- Step 2: Group Activity. In small groups, students will brainstorm and select a hook technique for a given topic. Each group will present their chosen hook and explain why it is effective.- Step 3: Peer Review and Feedback. Groups will provide feedback on each other's hooks, focusing on engagement, relevance, and clarity.

ILO: Develop a logical flow in a lesson plan that ensures a smooth transition between different segments of the lesson.
TC: Creating Logical Flow in Lesson Plans- Step 1: Understanding Segmentation. Introduce the concept of segmenting a lesson into distinct parts (e.g., introduction, main body, conclusion).- Step 2: Transition Techniques. Discuss and demonstrate various transition techniques (e.g., summarizing, previewing, using connecting phrases).- Step 3: Practical Exercise. Students will create a detailed lesson plan with clear transitions between segments. They will then present their plans, and the class will provide feedback on the logical flow and transitions.

ILO: Evaluate and refine a lesson plan to ensure it meets the learning objectives and engages the target audience.
TC: Evaluating and Refining Lesson Plans- Step 1: Criteria for Evaluation. Introduce criteria for evaluating a lesson plan (e.g., alignment with learning objectives, engagement, clarity, logical flow).- Step 2: Peer Review Session. Students will exchange their lesson plans and use the provided criteria to evaluate and provide constructive feedback.- Step 3: Revision and Presentation. Based on the feedback, students will revise their lesson plans and present the final version to the class, explaining the changes made and how they address the evaluation criteria.

ILO: Develop and execute a complete hook, body, and conclusion cycle for a project presentation within a strict 10-minute timeframe, ensuring clarity and coherence. Transferable Skills: Time Management, Oral Communication
TC: Time-Boxed Presentation Techniques: Teach students how to structure their presentations effectively within a 10-minute limit. - Hook (1 minute): Start with a compelling opening that captures the audience's attention. - Body (7 minutes): Clearly present the main points, using visual aids and concise language. - Conclusion (2 minutes): Summarize key takeaways and end with a strong closing statement. Practice sessions: Students will practice their presentations in small groups, receiving feedback on timing and clarity.

ILO: Apply time management strategies to allocate specific time slots for each section of a project report, ensuring the completion of all required components within a 4-hour writing session. Transferable Skills: Time Management, Written Communication
TC: Effective Time Allocation for Writing: Introduce techniques for managing time during a 4-hour writing session. - Planning (30 minutes): Outline the report, breaking it down into sections (introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion). - Writing (3 hours): Allocate specific time slots for each section, setting mini-deadlines. - Review (30 minutes): Use the remaining time for editing and proofreading. Tools and Templates: Provide templates and checklists to help students stay on track. Group Work: Students will work in pairs to review and provide feedback on each other's time allocation plans.

ILO: Implement a structured approach to manage and prioritize tasks for a group project, ensuring that all team members meet their deadlines and contribute effectively within a 4-week timeframe. Transferable Skills: Time Management, Team Collaboration
TC: Task Management and Prioritization: Teach students how to use project management tools and techniques to keep the team on schedule. - Project Timeline: Create a detailed timeline with milestones and deadlines for each task. - Task Assignment: Assign specific tasks to team members, ensuring everyone understands their responsibilities. - Regular Check-Ins: Schedule weekly meetings to review progress and address any issues. Tools: Introduce project management software (e.g., Trello, Asana) to help track tasks and deadlines. Case Study: Analyze a successful project timeline and discuss what made it effective. Role-Playing: Students will simulate a 4-week project, practicing task assignment and regular check-ins.

ILO: Break down a complex project into smaller, manageable tasks and create a detailed Gantt chart to visualize the project timeline. Transferable Skills: Project Management, Time Management
TC: Project Breakdown & Gantt Chart Creation: Guide students through the process of deconstructing a large project into smaller, achievable tasks. Use a step-by-step approach to identify and list all necessary tasks. Next, estimate the time required for each task and assign responsible team members. Finally, create a Gantt chart to visually represent the project timeline, including start and end dates, dependencies, and milestones.

ILO: Develop a comprehensive project risk management plan that identifies potential risks, assesses their impact, and outlines mitigation strategies. Transferable Skills: Risk Management, Critical Thinking
TC: Risk Management Plan Development: Teach students how to identify potential risks associated with their project. Use brainstorming sessions to generate a list of risks, then categorize them by likelihood and impact. For each identified risk, develop a detailed mitigation strategy, including preventive measures and contingency plans. Compile this information into a comprehensive risk management plan that can be used throughout the project lifecycle.

ILO: Create a stakeholder communication plan that includes key messages, communication channels, and a schedule for regular updates. Transferable Skills: Communication, Stakeholder Engagement
TC: Stakeholder Communication Plan Development: Instruct students on the importance of effective communication with stakeholders. Begin by identifying the key stakeholders and their specific needs and expectations. Develop key messages tailored to each stakeholder group. Choose appropriate communication channels (e.g., email, meetings, reports) and establish a schedule for regular updates. Create a detailed communication plan that outlines the frequency, content, and format of communications, ensuring that all stakeholders are kept informed and engaged.

ILO: Respond to audience questions in a concise and focused manner, ensuring that the answers align with the key messages of the presentation. Transferable Skills: Clear communication, adaptability
TC: Q&A Practice Session: \\ 1. Role-Play Q&A: Students practice answering potential questions from the audience, focusing on maintaining the core message. \\ 2. Peer Feedback: Peers provide feedback on clarity, conciseness, and alignment with the main points. \\ 3. Instructor Tips: Provide strategies for handling unexpected or challenging questions, such as pausing to think, rephrasing the question, and using bridging phrases.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of responses to audience questions by identifying areas for improvement in clarity, relevance, and brevity. Transferable Skills: Critical thinking, self-reflection
TC: Q&A Evaluation Exercise: \\ 1. Video Review: Students watch recordings of their Q&A sessions and evaluate their own responses. \\ 2. Self-Assessment: Use a checklist to assess the clarity, relevance, and brevity of each response. \\ 3. Group Discussion: Share insights and common challenges, and discuss strategies for improvement. \\ 4. Instructor Feedback: Provide individualized feedback and suggestions for refining Q&A skills.

ILO: Develop strategies for managing time effectively during Q&A sessions, ensuring that all questions are addressed within the allotted time. Transferable Skills: Time management, prioritization
TC: Time Management in Q&A: \\ 1. Time-Boxing Practice: Students practice answering questions within a set time limit (e.g., 1 minute per question). \\ 2. Prioritization Techniques: Teach students how to prioritize questions based on importance and relevance. \\ 3. Transition Phrases: Introduce phrases to help move smoothly between questions and manage the flow of the session. \\ 4. Simulation: Conduct a mock Q&A session with a strict time limit, followed by a debrief on time management strategies.

ILO: Craft a compelling narrative that effectively communicates the importance and urgency of a given issue, using persuasive language and emotional appeal to engage the audience.
TC: Narrative Development Workshop: \\- Step 1: Introduction to Persuasive Storytelling (10 mins): Discuss the key elements of a compelling narrative, including the use of emotional appeals, personal anecdotes, and vivid imagery. \\- Step 2: Case Study Analysis (15 mins): Analyze a real-world example of a persuasive narrative, breaking down its structure and identifying the techniques used. \\- Step 3: Group Activity (30 mins): Students work in small groups to develop a narrative around a specific issue, incorporating the elements discussed. Each group presents their narrative to the class. \\- Step 4: Peer and Instructor Feedback (15 mins): Peers and the instructor provide feedback on the narratives, focusing on clarity, engagement, and persuasiveness.

ILO: Construct a logical and evidence-based argument to support a call to action, using data and research to strengthen the case and address potential counterarguments.
TC: Argument Construction Exercise: \\- Step 1: Introduction to Logical Argumentation (10 mins): Review the components of a strong, evidence-based argument, including premises, conclusions, and the use of data. \\- Step 2: Data Collection and Analysis (20 mins): Students gather and analyze relevant data and research to support their argument. \\- Step 3: Argument Drafting (30 mins): Students draft their arguments, ensuring they include a clear call to action, supporting evidence, and responses to potential counterarguments. \\- Step 4: Peer Review and Refinement (20 mins): Students exchange drafts with peers for feedback, then refine their arguments based on the feedback received. \\- Step 5: Final Presentations (15 mins): Students present their refined arguments to the class, followed by a Q&A session.

ILO: Design and deliver a persuasive presentation that effectively uses visual aids, body language, and vocal delivery to enhance the message and influence the audience's perspective or behavior.
TC: Persuasive Presentation Skills Training: \\- Step 1: Introduction to Effective Presentation Techniques (10 mins): Discuss the importance of visual aids, body language, and vocal delivery in persuasive presentations. \\- Step 2: Visual Aid Design (20 mins): Students create visual aids (e.g., slides, charts, infographics) that support their arguments and enhance their presentations. \\- Step 3: Body Language and Vocal Delivery Practice (20 mins): Students practice their body language and vocal delivery through role-playing exercises, receiving feedback from peers and the instructor. \\- Step 4: Presentation Rehearsal (30 mins): Students rehearse their full presentations, incorporating all elements discussed. \\- Step 5: Final Presentations and Debrief (30 mins): Students deliver their final presentations to the class, followed by a debrief session where the instructor provides detailed feedback on each presentation.

ILO: Formulate concise, on-message responses to unexpected questions by quickly identifying core concerns and aligning answers with key project objectives. Transferable Skills: Adaptive communication, message consistency under pressure
TC: Q&A Response Framework & Practice - Introduce the 3C Framework: 1) Clarify (restate question to confirm understanding), 2) Connect (link to project goals/key messages), 3) Conclude (brief summary with next steps). Guide students through timed drills where they respond to challenging questions about their project proposals, focusing on staying within 60-second responses while maintaining alignment with their core problem statements and solutions.

ILO: Analyze question intent and stakeholder perspectives to craft targeted responses that address underlying concerns while reinforcing project value propositions. Transferable Skills: Stakeholder analysis, persuasive communication
TC: Intent Mapping & Response Tailoring - Teams practice identifying question types: clarification-seeking, challenge-based, or expansion requests. Using their stakeholder empathy maps, students role-play responding to questions from different stakeholder groups (e.g., funders asking about ROI, users questioning feasibility). Guide them to adapt responses by emphasizing relevant benefits: for funders highlight measurable outcomes, for users emphasize usability improvements.

ILO: Develop structured rebuttals to critical questions by anticipating objections, preparing evidence-backed counterpoints, and redirecting to project strengths. Transferable Skills: Critical thinking under pressure, evidence-based persuasion
TC: Objection Handling & Redirection Techniques - Introduce the A-E-R Method: Acknowledge (validate the concern), Evidence (provide 1-2 data points from research), Redirect (pivot to project strengths). Students practice with common project objections: 'This seems too ambitious' → acknowledge scope concerns, cite phased implementation plan, redirect to pilot success metrics. Conduct mock Q&A sessions with 'devil's advocate' questioning to build response fluency.

ILO: Structure project information into a compelling narrative arc with clear beginning, middle, and end, moving beyond factual lists to engage stakeholders emotionally and intellectually. Transferable Skills: Narrative Design, Audience Engagement
TC: Narrative Arc Construction Workshop - Step 1: Map project facts onto a 3-act structure (Setup: problem context, Confrontation: solution development, Resolution: outcomes/impact). Step 2: Transform data points into story elements (e.g., turn 'waste statistics' into 'community challenge scene', 'prototype testing' into 'innovation journey'). Step 3: Draft a 3-paragraph narrative summary connecting individual contributions to the overarching story.

ILO: Apply character development and conflict-resolution techniques to personify project elements (e.g., stakeholders, technologies, data) within a cohesive story framework. Transferable Skills: Creative Personification, Conflict Narrative Design
TC: Character & Conflict Narrative Exercise - Part A: Assign 'character roles' to project components (e.g., 'The Resilient Community' as protagonist, 'Waste Accumulation' as antagonist). Part B: Develop mini-stories showing conflicts/resolutions (e.g., 'How the Smart Bin technology overcame User Resistance through iterative design'). Part C: Create a storyboard linking 3-4 character interactions to demonstrate project evolution.

ILO: Utilize sensory language and emotional hooks to transform technical project details into vivid, memorable storytelling that maintains factual accuracy while enhancing persuasiveness. Transferable Skills: Descriptive Writing, Emotional Resonance
TC: Sensory Storytelling Lab - Activity 1: Rewrite 3 technical sentences using sensory descriptors (e.g., change 'The sensor detects waste levels' to 'The bin hums to life, its sensors whispering data about yesterday's consumption'). Activity 2: Identify emotional hooks in project milestones (e.g., 'breakthrough moment' during testing). Activity 3: Compose a 150-word story segment blending one technical aspect with one emotional appeal.

ILO: Formulate open-ended questions that explore multiple perspectives and assumptions in project scenarios to uncover deeper insights rather than seeking single correct answers.
TC: Question Design Workshop & Application: - Introduce open-ended vs. closed-ended questions with examples (e.g., "How might different stakeholders view this problem?" vs. "Is this solution correct?"). - Students analyze a provided project case study and draft 3 open-ended questions that probe underlying assumptions, stakeholder perspectives, or alternative approaches. - In small groups, share questions, receive peer feedback on their ability to stimulate discussion, and refine based on criteria (e.g., prompts critical thinking, avoids yes/no answers).

ILO: Apply probing questions to dissect complex problems, identify gaps in reasoning, and guide peers toward self-discovery during collaborative feedback sessions.
TC: Probing Question Practice in Peer Review: - Model probing techniques (e.g., "What evidence supports that conclusion?", "How does this align with the project's goals?") using a sample project section. - In pairs, students review a peer's project draft, using at least 2 probing questions to highlight areas for deeper analysis (e.g., "Can you explain the connection between your data and your proposed solution?"). - Groups discuss how these questions improved feedback quality, focusing on fostering critical reflection over direct correction.

ILO: Integrate questioning techniques into project discussions to facilitate inclusive dialogue, challenge assumptions, and drive iterative problem-solving without relying on instructor-led answers.
TC: Facilitated Group Dialogue Session: - Students lead a 15-minute discussion on a project milestone, using a mix of open-ended and probing questions to engage all members (e.g., "What are the potential risks we haven't considered?", "Why might this approach fail in a real-world context?"). - Peers evaluate the facilitator's questioning effectiveness based on criteria: stimulates multiple viewpoints, avoids lecturing, and encourages evidence-based responses. - Reflect on how questioning shifted the group's problem-solving process, emphasizing student-driven inquiry.

ILO: Design a 60-second lesson opening that establishes clear learning objectives while creating curiosity through a relevant hook (e.g., provocative question, brief story, surprising fact). Transferable Skills: Instructional Design (sub-skill: objective-hook integration for engagement)
TC: Set Induction Design Framework: Guide students through a structured approach to create effective lesson openings. First, analyze the core learning objective of the session and identify one key question or concept to highlight. Then, select a hook type (e.g., anecdote, question, data point) that directly relates to this objective and can be delivered within 60 seconds. Finally, practice sequencing: state the hook, briefly connect it to the objective, and outline the session's flow, ensuring logical progression and time management.

ILO: Apply audience analysis techniques to tailor the set induction's content and delivery style for specific learner profiles (e.g., prior knowledge, interests, cultural context). Transferable Skills: Audience Adaptation (sub-skill: customization for diverse learners)
TC: Audience-Centric Hook Development: This module focuses on adapting set inductions to learner characteristics. Begin by having students create a quick learner profile for a hypothetical or real audience, noting factors like background knowledge and motivations. Then, guide them to modify a standard hook (e.g., a technical example) to better resonate with this profile—for instance, simplifying jargon or adding relatable analogies. Finally, practice delivering the tailored hook within the 60-second constraint, emphasizing clarity and engagement.

ILO: Evaluate and refine a set induction draft using criteria such as clarity, relevance, engagement, and time efficiency, incorporating peer feedback for improvement. Transferable Skills: Critical Evaluation (sub-skill: iterative refinement based on feedback)
TC: Set Induction Critique and Iteration: Prepare students to enhance their lesson openings through evaluation. First, introduce a rubric with criteria: clarity of objective, hook relevance, engagement level, and adherence to 60 seconds. Then, in pairs or small groups, have students present their draft set inductions and receive structured feedback using the rubric. Finally, guide them to revise their drafts based on insights, focusing on tightening the flow, strengthening the hook, and ensuring the opening logically leads into the main lesson content.

ILO: Deliver immediate, constructive feedback that identifies specific strengths and areas for improvement, using clear examples to guide the learner's progress.
TC: Immediate & Constructive Feedback Techniques- Key strategies for Reinforcement & Feedback: 1. Use the "Sandwich Method" (praise → correction → encouragement) with real-time examples: e.g., "Your data analysis is thorough (strength), but the conclusion lacks stakeholder impact (area for improvement); try linking findings to user needs for clarity (guidance)." 2. Provide specific, actionable corrections: Instead of "Good job," say "Your prototype's user interface is intuitive because of the simplified navigation (specific praise); to enhance it, add a feedback button for immediate user input (constructive correction)."

ILO: Apply feedback loops to adjust learning strategies and project outcomes, ensuring continuous improvement based on learner responses and performance data.
TC: Feedback Loops & Adaptive Learning- Workshop on Reinforcement & Feedback: 1. Teach feedback cycles: e.g., "Observe learner's progress → Provide immediate correction → Monitor adjustments → Reinforce improvements." 2. Use data-driven examples: e.g., "If a learner struggles with market analysis, offer a mini-case study on pricing strategies (correction), then praise their revised analysis (reinforcement)."- Practice session: Simulate scenarios where learners give and receive feedback on project milestones, focusing on timely adjustments to tasks based on peer input.

ILO: Foster a supportive feedback environment by balancing praise and correction to motivate learners and enhance collaborative learning outcomes.
TC: Balanced Feedback for Motivation & Collaboration- Key strategies: 1. Balance ratio: Aim for 3:1 praise-to-correction in group settings to maintain engagement. 2. Use collaborative examples: e.g., "In team discussions, praise active listening (e.g., 'You summarized key points well'), then correct unclear communication (e.g., 'Try rephrasing technical terms for broader understanding')."- Activity: Role-play feedback sessions where learners practice giving constructive praise and correction in pairs, followed by group reflection on how feedback improved task alignment and team dynamics.

ILO: Apply open gestures and purposeful movement to project confidence and engage the audience during presentations.
TC:
Confidence-Building Movement Workshop: Focus on Open Gestures & Stage Presence
1. 5-Minute Movement Demonstration: Instructor models effective body language techniques:
   - "How do open palms and expansive arm movements convey confidence and openness?"
   - "What role does purposeful movement across the stage play in maintaining audience engagement?"
2. 3-Minute Peer Observation: Students practice while peers use a checklist to identify:
   - "Are gestures open and away from the body (template requirement)?"
   - "Does movement appear natural and connected to speech content?"
3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback: Provide specific examples of how to adjust posture and movement to build rapport.

ILO: Self-evaluate body language effectiveness using video recordings and a structured rubric to identify areas for improvement.
TC:
Body Language Self-Assessment Lab
Use a video recording and rubric-based checklist:
Posture & Stance: Is weight balanced? Are shoulders relaxed and open?
Gestures: Are hands visible and gestures purposeful? Do they complement verbal messages?
Movement: Is there purposeful use of space? Does movement enhance connection with different audience sections?
Log specific observations (e.g., "frequent crossed arms during Q&A") for targeted practice.

ILO: Integrate Session 1's vocal projection techniques and Session 2's eye contact strategies with body language to create cohesive, confident stage presence.
TC:
Integrated Presence Development: Body Language & Vocal/Eye Contact Alignment
- Recap Check: Quick review of key concepts:
  Session 1: Vocal projection techniques (breath support, volume modulation).
  Session 2: Eye contact strategies (scanning patterns, holding gaze for connection).
- Integration Practice: Use a "Presence-Integration Matrix" to combine skills:
  ① Practice delivering a short pitch while synchronizing open gestures with vocal emphasis points.
  ② Incorporate purposeful movement to different audience zones while maintaining consistent eye contact.

ILO: Execute a complete project cycle (hook, body, conclusion) within a strict 15-minute timeframe, demonstrating rapid planning and delivery.
TC: - Hook-Body-Conclusion Sprint (15 mins): Students must outline and present a mini-project proposal in 15 minutes: Hook (2 mins): Craft a compelling opening that states the core problem. Body (10 mins): Develop the main solution with 2-3 key points and supporting details. Conclusion (3 mins): Summarize outcomes and next steps. - Time-Boxed Phases: Use a timer to enforce strict limits for each phase (e.g., 2 mins for hook, 10 mins for body, 3 mins for conclusion). - Peer Time-Keeping: Assign peers to monitor and provide feedback on time adherence and cycle completeness.

ILO: Prioritize and allocate time effectively across project phases (hook, body, conclusion) under narrow constraints, ensuring balanced focus and completion.
TC: - Time Allocation Workshop (10 mins): Teach students to break down the 15-minute cycle: Hook (20% of time): Focus on clarity and engagement. Body (60% of time): Develop core content with evidence. Conclusion (20% of time): Reinforce key messages and actions. - Prioritization Exercise: Students list 3 critical elements for each phase and allocate time proportionally (e.g., "Spend 3 mins on solution details in body"). - Simulation Practice: Conduct timed drills where students adjust allocations based on peer feedback to optimize cycle flow.

ILO: Adapt and refine project delivery in real-time to meet strict deadlines, enhancing agility and time-sensitive execution skills.
TC: - Real-Time Adaptation Drill (15 mins): Students practice delivering a project cycle with mid-session adjustments: Start with a 5-minute plan, then receive a "time crunch" scenario (e.g., "Reduce body by 2 minutes") and must adapt on the fly. - Feedback Loop: Peers provide immediate feedback on time management and cycle coherence post-drill. - Reflection and Adjustment: Students document 1-2 strategies used to compress or expand sections without losing key content (e.g., "Condensed solution points by using bullet lists").

ILO: Design and implement 2-minute 'Think-Pair-Share' activities at key content transitions to maintain learner focus and assess real-time comprehension. Transferable Skills: Active listening, collaborative learning, formative assessment
TC: Engagement Activity Design & Implementation- Activity Framework: Introduce the 'Think-Pair-Share' structure:① Think (30 sec): Individual reflection on a key concept just covered.② Pair (60 sec): Discuss insights with a partner.③ Share (30 sec): Volunteers report out key takeaways.- Implementation Points: Identify 3 natural content breaks in the session (e.g., after introducing a new methodology, before case study analysis, during solution brainstorming).- Check-for-Understanding: Use shared responses to identify knowledge gaps and adjust pacing accordingly.

ILO: Create and facilitate brief 'Minute Paper' reflections at session midpoints to capture student questions and gauge understanding of complex concepts. Transferable Skills: Metacognition, concise communication, formative feedback collection
TC: Reflective Checkpoint Design- Minute Paper Protocol: Guide students to write for 60 seconds answering:① What is the clearest point about [current topic]?② What question remains unanswered?- Implementation Timing: Schedule at the 25-minute mark of a 50-minute session, immediately following explanation of a challenging concept (e.g., stakeholder analysis frameworks).- Response Utilization: Collect and quickly categorize responses to address common misconceptions in real-time before proceeding.

ILO: Integrate rapid 'Fist-to-Five' consensus checks during group decision-making processes to ensure all voices are heard and collective understanding is verified. Transferable Skills: Democratic participation, consensus building, non-verbal communication
TC: Consensus Building Activities- Fist-to-Five Protocol: Teach the visual scale:① Fist (0): Complete disagreement/confusion.② 1-3 fingers: Partial understanding/agreement.③ 4-5 fingers: Strong agreement/understanding.- Application Scenarios: Use during group work sessions when teams must:① Prioritize project tasks (check agreement on importance).② Evaluate solution feasibility (check understanding of constraints).③ Allocate team roles (check comfort with assignments).- Follow-up Actions: For any participant showing ≤2 fingers, facilitate 30-second clarification before proceeding.

ILO: Analyze the audience's background and expertise to adapt communication style, selecting appropriate tone, technical depth, and vocabulary for effective engagement.
TC: Audience Profiling & Communication Adaptation- Step 1: Audience Analysis Workshop. Guide students to profile their listeners using an "Audience Matrix" (expertise level × needs): Key factors: Professional background (e.g., technical vs. non-technical), prior knowledge of the topic, specific interests (e.g., practical applications vs. theoretical insights), and communication preferences (e.g., formal vs. informal). Groups identify 2–3 key audience characteristics for their project presentation.- Step 2: Communication Strategy Development. For each audience characteristic, students draft tailored approaches: 1) Tone adjustment (e.g., "Use conversational language for a general audience, technical jargon for experts"), 2) Depth control (e.g., "Provide high-level overviews for novices, detailed data for specialists"), 3) Vocabulary selection (e.g., "Avoid acronyms for mixed groups, define them clearly"). Practice with mock scenarios to refine adaptation.

ILO: Tailor presentation content and delivery to different stakeholder groups (e.g., peers, faculty, industry partners), ensuring clarity and relevance based on audience expertise. Transferable Skill: Contextual Communication, Stakeholder Engagement
TC: Stakeholder-Specific Content Customization. Self/peer-review for audience alignment: Check for mismatches (e.g., "Too technical for a business audience," "Lacks depth for academic reviewers"). Adjust content elements: Simplify complex concepts with analogies for non-experts, add technical details for specialists, and highlight benefits relevant to each stakeholder (e.g., emphasize innovation for industry, methodology for faculty). Log adaptations (e.g., "Add a glossary for mixed audiences," "Focus on practical outcomes for partners").

ILO: Integrate audience analysis into collaborative projects, explaining how tailored communication enhances both individual contributions and group objectives. Transferable Skills: Adaptive Communication, Team-Based Audience Targeting
TC: Prompt each team member to assess their primary audience for project tasks (e.g., "I present to engineers—need detailed specs," "I report to community groups—use simple language"). Discuss integration strategies: For example, a member targeting technical peers can provide in-depth data that supports another member's high-level summary for management. Draft 1–2 sentences per member linking their audience focus to the group's overall communication plan (e.g., "My simplified explanations will help the group's public outreach section").

ILO: Apply visual design principles (contrast, alignment, repetition, proximity) to create slides with clean layouts that enhance speech clarity and maintain audience focus.
TC: Visual Design Principles for Professional Slides- Step 1: Core Design Principles. Teach key visual design principles tailored to presentation slides:    a. Contrast: Use size, color, and font weight to highlight key points (e.g., bold headings vs. light body text).     b. Alignment: Ensure consistent left/center alignment for text and images to create visual order.   c. Repetition: Reuse colors, fonts, and layouts across slides for cohesion.                 d. Proximity: Group related elements (e.g., text and images) close together to show relationships.- 2: Slide Layout Practice. Demonstrate how to design clean slide layouts:   a. Create a template with a clear hierarchy (title → subtitle → bullet points → visuals).  b. Use white space effectively to avoid clutter and improve readability.  c. Apply principles to example slides (e.g., redesign a cluttered slide into a clean version).Students practice designing slides with these principles using tools like PowerPoint or Canva.

ILO: Select and integrate appropriate visual elements (e.g., icons, charts, images) that support speech content without distracting, ensuring professional aesthetics.
TC: Visual Element Integration for Effective Slides- Element Selection: Teams choose visuals that align with speech topics:① Use icons to represent concepts (e.g., a lightbulb for "ideas").② Incorporate charts/graphs for data presentation (e.g., bar charts for comparisons).③ Select high-quality images that reinforce messages (e.g., relevant photos for case studies).- Integration Techniques: Apply methods to blend visuals seamlessly:① Size and position visuals to complement text (e.g., place icons next to bullet points).② Use consistent color schemes and styles across all visuals.③ Avoid overloading slides; limit to 1-2 key visuals per slide.Groups practice creating slides with integrated visuals and receive feedback on clarity and supportiveness.

ILO: Iterate slide designs based on peer feedback to refine professionalism and speech alignment, ensuring slides enhance rather than detract from oral delivery.
TC: Slide Design Iteration for Professional Refinement- Feedback Integration: Teams revise their slides using peer critiques:① Identify distractions (e.g., busy backgrounds, inconsistent fonts).② Assess speech support (e.g., do visuals clarify or confuse points?).③ Check professionalism (e.g., are colors and layouts appropriate for academic/business contexts?).- Refinement Steps: Implement changes to improve slides:① Simplify layouts by removing unnecessary elements.② Adjust visual hierarchy to emphasize key speech moments.③ Test slides with speech practice to ensure timing and focus align.Groups iterate on slide sets, documenting changes and justifying design choices for improved outcomes.

ILO: Apply the Clarity of Explanation framework (simple language, precise terminology, relevant examples) to articulate a mini-concept from their project, ensuring comprehension by diverse stakeholders. Transferable Skills: Communication, Audience Adaptation
TC: Mini-Concept Explanation Workshop: 1. Framework Introduction: Review Clarity of Explanation components: simple language (avoid jargon), precise terminology (define key terms), relevant examples (tailored to audience). 2. Concept Selection: Each student selects one mini-concept from their project (e.g., "AI algorithm's decision-making process"). 3. Drafting Exercise: Write a 3-sentence explanation using the framework: simple language (e.g., "The AI learns patterns"), precise terminology (e.g., "machine learning model"), relevant examples (e.g., "like how it identifies recyclables in waste sorting"). 4. Peer Review: Exchange drafts for feedback on clarity gaps (e.g., "jargon 'neural network' unclear without example").

ILO: Use simple, precise language and relevant examples to refine a complex project insight into a clear, actionable statement for the Project Brief. Transferable Skill: Critical Thinking, Synthesis
TC: Insight Refinement Session: 1. Insight Analysis: Review a complex project insight (e.g., "Stakeholder interviews reveal cognitive overload in waste sorting decisions"). 2. Clarity Application: Apply Clarity of Explanation: simplify language (e.g., "People get confused when sorting trash"), add precision (e.g., "due to too many recycling categories"), provide examples (e.g., "like mixing plastic types"). 3. Drafting Practice: Rewrite the insight into a clear statement (e.g., "Residents struggle with waste sorting because complex rules cause confusion, such as distinguishing between plastic #1 and #2"). 4. Group Feedback: Discuss revisions to ensure the statement is understandable and actionable for the Project Brief.

ILO: Validate explanations of project solutions by ensuring they use simple, precise language and relevant examples to demonstrate feasibility and impact to peers. Transferable Skill: Persuasion, Evidence-Based Communication
TC: Solution Explanation Validation: 1. Solution Presentation: Each student presents one project solution (e.g., "Implement smart bins with sensors"). 2. Clarity Checklist: Use a checklist to evaluate: simple language (e.g., "bins detect items"), precise terminology (e.g., "IoT sensors"), relevant examples (e.g., "like how they alert when full"). 3. Peer Assessment: Peers provide feedback on gaps (e.g., "example needed for sensor accuracy"). 4. Revision Round: Students revise explanations based on feedback, focusing on enhancing clarity (e.g., "Smart bins use IoT sensors to detect waste types, such as identifying plastic bottles via infrared scans, improving sorting accuracy by 30%").

ILO: Design and deliver a persuasive pitch that clearly calls the audience to action by the end of the session.
TC: Persuasive Pitch Development Workshop: Focus on crafting a compelling call-to-action (CTA) : For each student: 1. 5-Minute Pitch Draft Presentation: The student presents their draft pitch, answering: - "How does my pitch structure build toward a clear CTA (e.g., using problem-solution-benefit framework)?" - "What specific action am I asking the audience to take (e.g., adopt a solution, change a behavior, support a proposal)?" 2. 3-Minute Peer Feedback: Peers evaluate persuasiveness (e.g., "The CTA is vague; suggest specifying 'sign this petition by Friday' instead of 'take action'"; "The emotional appeal in the middle section strengthens the CTA's impact"). 3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback: Provide examples of effective CTAs from real-world scenarios and suggest refinements.

ILO: Apply rhetorical strategies (e.g., ethos, pathos, logos) to shift audience perspective on a contentious issue.
TC: Rhetorical Strategy Application Session: Focus on using ethos, pathos, and logos to influence perspectives : - Step 1: Strategy Introduction. Present a framework: 1) Ethos (credibility: cite experts, data sources), 2) Pathos (emotional appeal: stories, vivid language), 3) Logos (logic: facts, reasoning). - Step 2: Group Persuasion Exercise. Groups develop a 3-minute argument on a given issue (e.g., "Implement sustainable practices in our community"): a. Identify the target audience's current perspective (e.g., skeptical about cost). b. Integrate all three strategies to shift it (e.g., use logos with cost-benefit data, pathos with a personal story, ethos by quoting a renowned environmentalist). c. Practice delivery with emphasis on persuasive tone and body language. Instructor reviews for balanced strategy use and effectiveness in perspective shift.

ILO: Evaluate and refine persuasive messages based on audience analysis to enhance influence.
TC: Audience-Centric Persuasion Review: Focus on tailoring messages to specific audience segments : For each student: 1. 5-Minute Audience Analysis Presentation: The student presents their persuasive message, answering: - "Who is my target audience (e.g., demographics, values, potential objections)?" - "How have I adapted my message to resonate with this audience (e.g., using jargon-free language for laypersons, highlighting benefits aligned with their interests)?" 2. 3-Minute Peer Feedback: Peers assess alignment (e.g., "The technical details may confuse non-expert audiences; simplify for better influence"; "The appeal to community values effectively addresses audience concerns"). 3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback: Provide examples of successful audience-tailored campaigns and suggest adjustments for greater impact.

ILO: Design and implement a visual learning path using presentation slides that sequentially builds concepts from foundational to advanced levels, with clear visual cues for each transition. Transferable Skills: Visual communication, instructional design
TC: Visual Learning Path Design: Prepare a slide deck for a 15-minute concept presentation- Slide Structure: Create 5-7 slides that follow this progression:① Title slide with key concept visual.② Foundational definition with simple diagram.③ Core principles with comparative charts.④ Application examples with annotated screenshots.⑤ Advanced implications with flowcharts.⑥ Summary slide with visual recap.- Visual Cues: Use consistent color coding (e.g., blue for definitions, green for applications), numbered steps for processes, and arrows to show relationships between elements. Test the deck by presenting to a peer and adjusting based on clarity feedback.

ILO: Utilize physical props or interactive whiteboards to demonstrate complex processes or relationships, ensuring the visual aids directly support and reinforce verbal explanations. Transferable Skills: Hands-on demonstration, real-time visual reinforcement
TC: Interactive Demonstration Setup: Conduct a 10-minute process explanation using props or whiteboard- Prop/Board Preparation: Select 3-5 physical objects (e.g., models, cards, tools) or prepare a whiteboard diagram in advance. For example, use colored blocks to represent data flow in a system, or draw a timeline on the board for project phases.- Demonstration Steps:① Introduce the process verbally while pointing to each prop/board element.② Move or modify props/board drawings in real-time to show changes (e.g., rearrange blocks to illustrate feedback loops, add annotations to the timeline).③ Pause at key points to ask audience questions based on the visual aids, ensuring understanding.④ Conclude by summarizing the process using the props/board as a reference, and provide a handout with photos or sketches of the setup for review.

ILO: Integrate multiple instructional aids (e.g., slides, boards, and props) in a single session to create a cohesive and multi-sensory learning experience, aligning each aid with specific learning objectives. Transferable Skills: Multi-modal instruction, learning environment design
TC: Multi-Aid Integration Workshop: Plan and execute a 20-minute teaching segment using combined aids- Aid Coordination: Map out which aid supports each objective:① Use slides for overview and key definitions (first 5 minutes).② Switch to whiteboard for interactive problem-solving or brainstorming (next 10 minutes).③ Introduce props for hands-on application or case study demonstration (final 5 minutes).- Seamless Transitions: Practice moving between aids smoothly—e.g., display a slide with a diagram, then replicate it on the whiteboard for group annotation, followed by using props to simulate the diagram in action. After the session, reflect on effectiveness by noting which aids best engaged learners and adjust future plans accordingly.

ILO: Deliver a 5-minute speech with controlled pacing, using strategic pauses to emphasize key points and eliminate filler words like 'um' or 'uh'.
TC: - Step 1: Pause & Emphasis Techniques. Introduce the "Strategic Pause Framework": 1) Transition Pauses (between main ideas), 2) Emphasis Pauses (before/after key statements), 3) Reflection Pauses (after complex points). Demonstrate with a sample speech, highlighting where pauses replace filler words.- Step 2: Speech Delivery Practice. Students prepare and deliver a 5-minute project update speech: a. Script the speech with marked pause points (e.g., "After explaining the prototype design [PAUSE] we will discuss user feedback"). b. Practice using a timer and filler-word counter (e.g., Feishu's speech analysis tool). c. Record the speech, focusing on maintaining flow without fillers. Instructor provides feedback on pause effectiveness and filler word elimination.

ILO: Structure persuasive arguments in oral presentations with clear rhetorical devices, maintaining fluency through planned transitions and avoiding verbal hesitations.
TC: Rhetorical Structure & Fluency Enhancement- Key strategies for persuasive speaking: 1. Use rhetorical devices: Repetition for emphasis (e.g., "Our solution is innovative, our solution is feasible"), Analogies to clarify complex ideas (e.g., "This AI model works like a skilled translator"). 2. Plan transitions: Employ phrases like "Building on that point..." or "This leads to our next finding..." to connect sections smoothly.- Key strategies for fluency: 1. Eliminate filler words: Practice with sentence starters (e.g., "In summary..." instead of "Um, so..."). 2. Use breath control: Incorporate brief pauses at commas and periods to replace hesitations. Students apply these in a 7-minute persuasive pitch for their project, with peers noting filler word usage and transition effectiveness.

ILO: Assess speech delivery against fluency criteria, identifying instances of effective pause usage and filler word patterns to refine public speaking skills.
TC: Speech Analysis & Feedback Session (Focus: Fluency & Rhetoric): For each student presenter: 1. 5-Minute Recorded Speech Playback: The student presents a segment of their project proposal orally, recorded via Feishu. Peers and instructor review for: a. Pause effectiveness (e.g., "Pause after 'critical finding' emphasized importance"). b. Filler word frequency (e.g., counted 'uh' occurrences using a tally sheet). 2. 3-Minute Peer Feedback: Peers highlight strengths and gaps (e.g., "Strong use of pauses at transitions, but filler words increased during technical explanations"). 3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback: Provide targeted improvements with examples, such as replacing filler words with planned pauses or restructuring sentences for smoother delivery.
