ILO: Apply vocal variety techniques (pitch modulation, pace variation, volume control) to enhance audience engagement and emphasize critical information in project presentations. Transferable Skills: Public Speaking (sub-skill: vocal modulation for emphasis)
TC: Vocal Variety Fundamentals & Application- Workshop on Vocal Modulation Techniques:1. Pitch Modulation: Teach how to vary pitch to convey emotion and importance (e.g., rising pitch for questions, lower pitch for serious points). Practice with contrasting statements: "Our solution is innovative" (high pitch for excitement) vs. "The data shows a critical risk" (low pitch for gravity).2. Pace Variation: Demonstrate slowing down for key points and speeding up for background information. Use exercises like reading a project summary with intentional pauses before main findings.3. Volume Control: Explain using volume to command attention (louder for emphasis) and create intimacy (softer for confidential insights). Practice with a scripted project update, adjusting volume for different sections.- Application Exercise: In groups, students revise a 2-minute project pitch to incorporate all three techniques, then present and receive peer feedback on effectiveness.

ILO: Analyze and adjust vocal delivery in real-time based on audience feedback cues (e.g., engagement levels, confusion signs) to maintain interest and clarity throughout a presentation.
TC: Audience-Centric Vocal Adaptation- Interactive Session on Reading Audience Cues:1. Teach identification of engagement indicators: Positive (nodding, eye contact) vs. negative (fidgeting, looking away). Use video examples from past project presentations to practice spotting cues.2. Link cues to vocal adjustments: For low engagement, increase volume or vary pace; for confusion, slow down and use clearer pitch articulation. Role-play scenarios where students present to a simulated "disengaged" audience and adapt on the fly.- Practice with Feedback Loops: In pairs, students deliver a 3-minute segment of their project proposal while observers note audience cues. Afterward, discuss and implement one vocal change based on the feedback, then re-present for improvement assessment.

ILO: Integrate vocal variety with visual aids and body language to create a cohesive and persuasive presentation style that reinforces key messages. Transferable Skills: Nonverbal Communication (synchronizing vocal and visual elements)
TC: Holistic Presentation Integration- Workshop on Synchronizing Delivery Elements:1. Align vocal techniques with slide content: For example, use a pause and volume increase when revealing a key data point on a slide, or vary pitch to match the emotional tone of an image (e.g., hopeful solution vs. urgent problem).2. Coordinate with body language: Teach how gestures (e.g., pointing) can coincide with vocal emphasis, and posture changes (leaning in) can enhance volume shifts for intimacy. Practice with a sample project overview, integrating vocal variety with simple gestures and slide transitions.- Group Synthesis Activity: In project teams, students design a 5-minute presentation segment that combines vocal variety (pitch, pace, volume), 2-3 key slides, and planned body language. Peers evaluate using a rubric focusing on cohesion and emphasis of main points, followed by a revision round to refine integration.

ILO: Deconstruct complex project tasks into sequential, manageable steps using a task breakdown framework, ensuring logical progression and clear dependencies.
TC: Task Decomposition Framework for Complex Projects- Step 1: Identify Core Components. Guide students to analyze a complex project (e.g., designing an educational app) and list its major components (e.g., research, design, development, testing).- Step 2: Break Down into Subtasks. Teach a hierarchical breakdown method: a. For each component, create subtasks (e.g., under "research": literature review, user interviews, data analysis). b. Further divide subtasks into actionable steps (e.g., "user interviews": draft questions, schedule sessions, conduct interviews, transcribe notes).- Step 3: Sequence and Dependencies. Use a flowchart or timeline tool (e.g., Miro) to: a. Arrange steps in logical order (e.g., research before design). b. Mark dependencies (e.g., "transcribe notes" must follow "conduct interviews").- Step 4: Assign and Monitor. Practice assigning subtasks to group members with deadlines, using Feishu Tasks to track progress and adjust as needed.

ILO: Structure multi-stage research processes into phased activities (e.g., preparation, execution, synthesis) to build understanding incrementally and avoid overwhelm.
TC: Phased Research Process Design- Phase 1: Preparation. Teach students to: a. Define research objectives (e.g., "understand user pain points"). b. Break objectives into small, focused questions (e.g., "What are the top 3 challenges teachers face?"). c. Plan resources (e.g., allocate 2 hours for interview prep).- Phase 2: Execution. Guide incremental data collection: a. Conduct one interview at a time, with debriefs after each to refine approach. b. Use templates (e.g., interview guides) to standardize steps.- Phase 3: Synthesis. Break analysis into chunks: a. First, summarize key quotes from interviews. b. Then, group quotes into themes (e.g., "time management issues"). c. Finally, draft insights with evidence (e.g., "Theme X supported by 4 interview quotes").- Practice: Groups apply this to a mini-research project, reporting progress after each phase.

ILO: Develop complex arguments or solutions by building them layer-by-layer (e.g., from evidence to claims to recommendations), ensuring each layer logically supports the next.
TC: Layered Argument/Solution Development- Layer 1: Evidence Collection. Teach students to gather small pieces of evidence (e.g., data points, quotes, observations) and organize them in a shared document (e.g., Feishu Docs).- Layer 2: Claim Formation. Guide incremental claim-building: a. For each evidence piece, draft a simple claim (e.g., "Users need faster feedback"). b. Combine related claims into broader statements (e.g., "Efficiency is a key user need").- Layer 3: Recommendation Structuring. Break solutions into components: a. Start with a core idea (e.g., "Add a notification feature"). b. Add layers: feasibility (e.g., "Use existing app infrastructure"), impact (e.g., "Reduce response time by 50%"), and steps (e.g., "Prototype in 2 weeks").- Practice: Students work on a group proposal, presenting each layer for peer feedback before moving to the next.

ILO: Clearly explain the mini-concept using simple, precise language and relevant examples to ensure understanding among peers.
TC: Mini-Concept Explanation: Students will be given a mini-concept related to their project (e.g., 'sustainability in urban planning'). They will then prepare a 5-minute presentation that breaks down the concept into understandable parts, using clear language and relevant, real-world examples. The presentation should include a visual aid (e.g., a simple diagram or infographic) to enhance clarity.

ILO: Use analogies and metaphors effectively to simplify complex ideas and make them more relatable and understandable for the audience.
TC: Analogies and Metaphors: Students will be provided with a list of complex technical terms or concepts (e.g., 'machine learning', 'circular economy'). They will choose one term and create an analogy or metaphor that simplifies the concept. Each student will present their analogy or metaphor to the class, explaining why it is effective in making the concept more accessible. The class will provide feedback on the clarity and effectiveness of the analogies and metaphors.

ILO: Develop and deliver a concise, step-by-step guide to a process or procedure, ensuring that each step is clearly explained and easy to follow.
TC: Step-by-Step Guide: Students will select a process or procedure relevant to their project (e.g., 'conducting a user interview', 'creating a prototype'). They will develop a concise, step-by-step guide that includes clear, simple instructions for each step. The guide should also include tips and potential pitfalls to avoid. Students will present their guide to the class, demonstrating how to follow each step, and receive feedback on the clarity and comprehensibility of their instructions.

ILO: Understand the principles of visual design and apply them to create professional, clean, and effective slides that enhance the clarity and impact of a presentation.
TC: Introduction to Visual Design Principles: Discuss the importance of visual design in presentations. Introduce key principles such as simplicity, alignment, contrast, and consistency. Provide examples of good and bad slide designs. Students will practice applying these principles by redesigning a sample slide.

ILO: Develop the ability to use color, typography, and imagery effectively to support the message and maintain the audience's attention.
TC: Effective Use of Color, Typography, and Imagery: Explain how to choose and use colors, fonts, and images to enhance the visual appeal and readability of slides. Demonstrate the impact of different color schemes, font choices, and image types on the audience. Students will create a set of slides using provided templates, focusing on the effective use of these elements.

ILO: Apply best practices for data visualization to create clear and informative charts, graphs, and diagrams that support the presentation's key points.
TC: Data Visualization Best Practices: Teach students how to select and create appropriate data visualizations (charts, graphs, diagrams) to present information clearly and effectively. Cover common mistakes and best practices in data visualization. Students will work in groups to create a presentation with multiple data visualizations, receiving feedback on their effectiveness and clarity.

ILO: Effectively structure and deliver a persuasive speech, using rhetorical techniques to engage the audience and convey a clear message. Transferable Skills: Public Speaking, Rhetoric
TC: Introduction to Rhetorical Techniques- Step 1: Understanding Rhetoric. Teach the basics of rhetoric, including ethos, pathos, and logos. - Step 2: Structuring a Speech. Guide students through the components of an effective speech: introduction, body, and conclusion. - Step 3: Practice and Feedback. Have students prepare and deliver a short speech, followed by peer and instructor feedback.

ILO: Use pauses effectively and avoid filler words to enhance the clarity and impact of their spoken communication. Transferable Skills: Public Speaking, Clarity in Communication
TC: Mastering Pauses and Eliminating Fillers- Step 1: Importance of Pauses. Explain the role of pauses in emphasizing key points and improving listener comprehension. - Step 2: Identifying and Reducing Fillers. Provide examples of common filler words (e.g., um, uh, like) and strategies to reduce their use. - Step 3: Practical Exercises. Conduct exercises where students practice speaking with deliberate pauses and minimal fillers, followed by group feedback and self-assessment.

ILO: Develop and demonstrate the ability to handle questions and impromptu speaking situations with confidence and coherence. Transferable Skills: Public Speaking, Impromptu Speaking, Q&A Handling
TC: Handling Questions and Impromptu Speaking- Step 1: Preparing for Q&A. Teach techniques for anticipating and preparing for potential questions from the audience. - Step 2: Strategies for Impromptu Speaking. Provide tips for maintaining composure and coherence in impromptu speaking situations. - Step 3: Role-Playing Exercises. Engage students in role-playing activities where they practice answering unexpected questions and delivering impromptu speeches, with feedback from peers and the instructor.

ILO: Engage in a peer review activity to provide and receive constructive feedback on the clarity and coherence of the Project Brief. Transferable Skills: Communication, Critical Thinking
TC: Peer Review Activity for Project Briefs Divide students into pairs or small groups. Each student will share their Project Brief with their peers. Peers will use a provided rubric to evaluate the following aspects: Clarity of the problem statement, coherence of the proposed solutions, and feasibility of the next steps. After the review, students will discuss the feedback and make necessary revisions.

ILO: Participate in a think-pair-share activity to brainstorm and refine potential solutions for the identified problem. Transferable Skills: Collaboration, Creative Problem Solving
TC: Think-Pair-Share Activity for Solution Brainstorming Instruct students to individually brainstorm at least three potential solutions to the identified problem. Pair students up and have them share their ideas with each other. Together, they should select the most promising solution and refine it, considering feasibility, impact, and alignment with the project goals. Finally, each pair will present their refined solution to the class for further discussion.

ILO: Use a formative assessment quiz to check understanding of key concepts and criteria for the Project Brief. Transferable Skills: Self-Assessment, Knowledge Retention
TC: Formative Assessment Quiz on Project Brief Criteria Create a short quiz (5-10 questions) that covers the key components and criteria of the Project Brief template. The quiz should include multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer questions. Students will complete the quiz individually, and after submission, they will receive immediate feedback on their answers. Use the results to identify common areas of misunderstanding and address them in a follow-up discussion.

ILO: Develop the ability to handle Q&A sessions by formulating concise and on-message responses to unexpected questions, demonstrating adaptability and clear communication.
TC: Q&A Simulation: Students will participate in a simulated Q&A session where they will be asked unexpected questions about their project. They will practice responding concisely and staying on message. - Preparation: Students will prepare a list of potential questions and their corresponding answers. - Execution: In small groups, students will take turns asking and answering questions, with peers providing feedback on clarity, conciseness, and relevance.

ILO: Enhance critical thinking skills by analyzing and addressing complex questions in real-time, ensuring that responses are well-structured and aligned with the core message of the project.
TC: Critical Thinking Exercise: Students will engage in a structured exercise where they are presented with a series of complex, multi-faceted questions related to their project. - Question Analysis: Students will break down each question into its key components and identify the main points that need to be addressed. - Response Formulation: Students will draft concise, well-structured responses that address the core message of the project. - Peer Review: Students will share their responses with peers for feedback on clarity, structure, and alignment with the project's core message.

ILO: Improve the ability to manage Q&A sessions effectively by maintaining composure, managing time, and ensuring that all questions are addressed in a coherent and organized manner.
TC: Q&A Management Workshop: Students will learn and practice techniques for managing Q&A sessions effectively. - Time Management: Students will practice allocating time for different types of questions and ensuring that all questions are addressed within the given timeframe. - Composure Techniques: Students will learn and apply techniques for maintaining composure and confidence during Q&A sessions, such as deep breathing and positive self-talk. - Structured Responses: Students will practice structuring their responses to ensure coherence and organization, using tools like bullet points and key phrases to stay on track.

ILO: Effectively manage time to complete a structured presentation (hook, body, and conclusion) within a 5-minute timeframe. Transferable Skills: Time Management (sub-skill: efficient content delivery)
TC: Time-Boxed Presentation Practice This module focuses on teaching students how to structure and deliver a concise, impactful presentation within a strict 5-minute limit. Start with a brief overview of the essential components of a good presentation (hook, body, and conclusion). Next, provide a template or guide for each section, emphasizing brevity and clarity. Finally, have students practice their presentations in small groups, using a timer to ensure they stay within the 5-minute limit. Provide feedback on pacing, clarity, and effectiveness.

ILO: Prioritize and sequence key information to create a compelling and coherent narrative within a 5-minute presentation. Transferable Skills: Time Management (sub-skill: prioritization and sequencing)
TC: Prioritization and Sequencing Techniques Teach students how to prioritize and sequence key information effectively. Begin by discussing the importance of a clear narrative arc and how to identify the most critical points. Use examples to illustrate how to condense complex ideas into digestible segments. Introduce techniques such as the Rule of Three (three main points) and the Pyramid Principle (starting with the most important information). Have students apply these techniques to their presentations, then share and receive peer feedback to refine their sequencing.

ILO: Utilize visual aids and verbal cues to enhance the clarity and impact of a 5-minute presentation. Transferable Skills: Time Management (sub-skill: effective use of visual and verbal tools)
TC: Visual Aids and Verbal Cues for Impactful Presentations This module focuses on the effective use of visual aids and verbal cues to enhance the clarity and impact of a 5-minute presentation. Start by introducing the types of visual aids that can be used (e.g., slides, charts, images) and how to design them for maximum impact. Discuss the importance of verbal cues, such as pauses, tone, and emphasis, to keep the audience engaged. Provide examples and best practices for integrating visual aids and verbal cues. Have students incorporate these elements into their presentations and practice delivering them, receiving feedback from peers and instructors.

ILO: Design a lesson plan that includes a compelling and engaging set induction to capture learners' interest within the first 60 seconds.
TC: Lesson Plan Development: Set Induction Techniques - 1. Introduction to Set Induction: Explain the importance of capturing learners' interest at the beginning of a lesson. 2. Examples of Effective Set Inductions: Provide and discuss examples of various set induction techniques (e.g., story, question, demonstration, problem, etc.). 3. Individual Planning: Students create a set induction for a hypothetical lesson, focusing on making it engaging and relevant. 4. Peer Review: Students present their set inductions to peers, who provide feedback on the effectiveness and engagement level. 5. Instructor Feedback: Provide constructive feedback and suggestions for improvement.

ILO: Evaluate the logical flow and coherence of a lesson plan, ensuring that the set induction effectively leads into the main content.
TC: Lesson Plan Analysis: Logical Flow and Coherence - 1. Lesson Plan Templates: Introduce different lesson plan templates and their components. 2. Sample Lesson Plans: Provide sample lesson plans with varying degrees of logical flow and coherence. 3. Group Analysis: Students work in groups to analyze the provided lesson plans, focusing on the transition from the set induction to the main content. 4. Group Presentations: Each group presents their analysis, highlighting strengths and areas for improvement. 5. Instructor Feedback: Summarize key points and provide additional insights on maintaining a logical flow in lesson planning.

ILO: Incorporate peer and instructor feedback to refine and improve the set induction and overall lesson plan.
TC: Lesson Plan Refinement: Incorporating Feedback - 1. Feedback Session: Students receive and review feedback from both peers and the instructor on their initial lesson plans. 2. Revision Time: Students use the feedback to revise their set inductions and the overall lesson plan. 3. Revised Presentations: Students present their revised lesson plans, focusing on how they incorporated the feedback. 4. Final Peer Review: Peers provide final feedback on the revised lesson plans, emphasizing the effectiveness of the set induction and the logical flow. 5. Instructor Summary: Provide a summary of the key takeaways and any final recommendations for further improvement.

ILO: Develop and use open-ended questions to stimulate critical thinking and deeper understanding of a given topic. Transferable Skills: Questioning Techniques, Critical Thinking
TC: Introduce the concept of open-ended questions and their importance in fostering critical thinking. Provide examples of both open-ended and closed-ended questions. Have students brainstorm and generate open-ended questions related to a specific topic or problem. Facilitate a group discussion where students share their questions and discuss how they can be used to explore the topic more deeply.

ILO: Apply probing questions to guide peers in exploring and refining their ideas and solutions. Transferable Skills: Questioning Techniques, Peer Collaboration
TC: Explain the purpose and structure of probing questions. Provide a scenario or problem for students to work on in pairs. Instruct one student to present an initial idea or solution, while the other uses probing questions to help refine and deepen the idea. Rotate roles and repeat the exercise. Debrief as a class, discussing the effectiveness of the probing questions and how they helped to clarify and improve the ideas.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of different questioning techniques in promoting critical thinking and problem-solving. Transferable Skills: Questioning Techniques, Evaluation and Reflection
TC: Provide a set of case studies or scenarios that require critical thinking and problem-solving. Divide students into small groups and assign each group a different questioning technique (e.g., open-ended, probing, Socratic). Each group will use their assigned technique to discuss and solve the given scenario. Afterward, have each group present their approach and the outcomes. Conduct a whole-class discussion to compare and evaluate the effectiveness of each questioning technique in promoting critical thinking and problem-solving.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to use open gestures and movement to project confidence and build rapport with an audience, enhancing their overall presence in a professional setting. Transferable Skills: Body Language & Presence (sub-skill: projecting confidence and building rapport)
TC: Conduct a workshop on the fundamentals of body language and presence, focusing on the importance of open gestures and movement. Students will practice various techniques, such as maintaining eye contact, using expansive gestures, and moving confidently around the room. They will receive feedback from peers and the instructor to refine their skills.

ILO: Apply the principles of effective body language and presence in a simulated professional presentation, demonstrating the ability to engage and connect with the audience. Transferable Skills: Body Language & Presence (sub-skill: engaging and connecting with the audience)
TC: Students will prepare and deliver a short, 5-minute presentation on a topic of their choice. The focus will be on incorporating the body language and presence techniques learned in the previous session. After each presentation, the class will provide constructive feedback, and the instructor will offer specific guidance on how to improve engagement and connection with the audience.

ILO: Evaluate and provide constructive feedback on the body language and presence of peers during presentations, reinforcing the importance of these skills in professional settings. Transferable Skills: Body Language & Presence (sub-skill: providing and receiving feedback)
TC: After each student's presentation, the class will engage in a structured feedback session. Each student will provide written and verbal feedback to their peers, focusing on the use of body language and presence. The instructor will facilitate this process, ensuring that feedback is constructive and actionable. This exercise will help students develop their ability to both give and receive feedback effectively.

ILO: Analyze and understand the specific needs, expertise, and expectations of the target audience for a project presentation.
TC: - Step 1: Audience Identification. Identify the key stakeholders and their roles (e.g., clients, team members, academic advisors).- Step 2: Needs Assessment. Conduct a survey or interview to gather information about the audience's background, expertise, and expectations.- Step 3: Analysis Workshop. In a group setting, discuss and analyze the collected data to identify common themes and unique needs of the audience.

ILO: Tailor the tone, depth, and vocabulary of a project presentation to match the identified needs and expertise of the target audience.
TC: - Step 1: Tone and Depth Adjustment. Based on the audience analysis, adjust the tone and depth of the presentation. For example, use more technical terms for an expert audience and simpler language for a general audience.- Step 2: Vocabulary Selection. Choose appropriate vocabulary that aligns with the audience's level of understanding. Use jargon only if it is familiar to the audience.- Step 3: Peer Review. Present the adjusted presentation to peers who are familiar with the target audience. Gather feedback on the clarity and appropriateness of the tone, depth, and vocabulary.

ILO: Develop and deliver a project presentation that effectively communicates the project goals, methods, and outcomes to the target audience, ensuring alignment with their needs and expertise.
TC: - Step 1: Presentation Development. Create a structured presentation that includes an introduction, methodology, results, and conclusion, tailored to the audience's needs and expertise.- Step 2: Practice and Refinement. Practice the presentation in front of a small group of peers or mentors. Refine the content based on feedback to ensure it is clear and engaging.- Step 3: Final Delivery. Deliver the presentation to the target audience, using the refined content and delivery style. Follow up with a Q&A session to address any questions or concerns from the audience.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to modulate pitch, pace, and volume to maintain audience interest and emphasize key points in a presentation.
TC: Teach students how to vary their vocal delivery: \\[1] Explain the importance of pitch, pace, and volume in engaging an audience. \\[2] Provide examples of effective vocal variety in famous speeches or presentations. \\[3] Conduct a practice session where students deliver a short segment of their project presentation, focusing on varying their vocal delivery.

ILO: Apply vocal variety techniques to enhance the clarity and impact of key messages in a presentation.
TC: Guide students in applying vocal variety to their presentations: \\[1] Discuss how to use pitch to convey emotion and emphasis. \\[2] Teach the use of pacing to build tension and maintain interest. \\[3] Show how to adjust volume to highlight important points. \\[4] Have students practice these techniques with a specific section of their presentation, such as the introduction or conclusion.

ILO: Evaluate and provide feedback on the use of vocal variety in peer presentations to improve overall delivery.
TC: Facilitate a peer review session on vocal variety: \\[1] Pair students up and have them present a segment of their project to each other. \\[2] Provide a checklist for evaluating pitch, pace, and volume. \\[3] Have students give and receive constructive feedback on their vocal delivery. \\[4] Discuss common areas for improvement and share best practices.

ILO: Develop a compelling narrative that persuades the audience to support the proposed solution.
TC: - Storytelling Techniques (15 mins): Introduce key elements of persuasive storytelling, such as establishing a clear problem, presenting a relatable solution, and using emotional appeals.\n- Narrative Building (20 mins): Students work in groups to create a narrative for their project, incorporating the storytelling techniques discussed. Each group presents a 3-minute pitch to the class.\- Peer Feedback (10 mins): Classmates provide feedback on the effectiveness of the narratives, focusing on clarity, engagement, and persuasiveness.

ILO: Construct and deliver a persuasive argument that effectively addresses counterarguments and strengthens the case for the proposed solution.
TC: - Anticipating Counterarguments (15 mins): Discuss common counterarguments related to the project and strategies for addressing them, such as providing evidence, acknowledging concerns, and reframing the issue.\- Argument Construction (20 mins): Students individually or in pairs develop a structured argument for their project, including a clear thesis, supporting points, and responses to potential counterarguments.\- Persuasive Speech (15 mins): Students present their arguments, and the class engages in a Q&A session to test the robustness of the arguments and provide constructive feedback.

ILO: Utilize rhetorical devices and persuasive language to enhance the impact of the presentation and influence the audience's perspective.
TC: - Rhetorical Devices (15 mins): Teach students about rhetorical devices such as ethos, pathos, and logos, and how to use them effectively in a presentation.\- Persuasive Language (15 mins): Provide examples of powerful and persuasive language, and have students practice rewriting parts of their presentations to incorporate these techniques.\- Practice and Refinement (20 mins): Students practice their presentations, focusing on the use of rhetorical devices and persuasive language. Peers and the instructor provide feedback on the effectiveness of the language and delivery.

ILO: Provide immediate, constructive feedback to peers on their project progress and deliverables using a structured feedback framework.
TC: - Step 1: Feedback Framework Introduction. Introduce the "Feedback Framework" which includes sections for: 1) Positive Reinforcement (what went well), 2) Constructive Criticism (areas for improvement), and 3) Next Steps (specific actions to take).- Step 2: Peer Review Session. Students will review and provide feedback on a peer's project deliverable using the Feedback Framework. Each student will submit their feedback to the instructor for review and additional comments.

ILO: Use formative assessment techniques to monitor and guide the progress of a team member's work, providing timely and actionable feedback.
TC: - Step 1: Formative Assessment Techniques. Teach students about formative assessment techniques such as checklists, rubrics, and one-on-one meetings. Provide examples and templates.- Step 2: Team Member Monitoring. Assign each student to monitor a specific team member's progress over the next week. They will use the formative assessment techniques to provide regular, actionable feedback. The monitored student will also provide feedback on the quality and helpfulness of the feedback received.

ILO: Implement a continuous feedback loop within the team to ensure that all members are aligned with the project goals and are making consistent progress.
TC: - Step 1: Continuous Feedback Loop Setup. Introduce the concept of a continuous feedback loop and its importance in project management. Discuss how to set up a feedback loop using tools like Feishu, Miro, or Trello.- Step 2: Feedback Loop Implementation. Each team will set up a continuous feedback loop using the chosen tool. This will include: 1) Regular check-ins (e.g., daily standups), 2) Weekly progress reports, and 3) Monthly retrospectives. The instructor will review the setup and provide feedback on its effectiveness and alignment with project goals.

ILO: Design and utilize instructional aids, such as boards, slides, or props, to enhance the visual learning experience and reinforce key concepts.
TC: Instructional Aids Design & Utilization- Key strategies for effective use of boards, slides, or props:1. Use clear, concise, and visually appealing visuals to support the content.2. Incorporate diagrams, charts, and images to illustrate complex ideas.3. Ensure that all visual aids are well-organized and easy to follow.- Practical exercises:1. Create a set of slides or a board presentation that complements a given lesson.2. Practice using props (e.g., models, real-world examples) to explain abstract concepts.3. Peer review and provide feedback on the effectiveness of each other's visual aids.

ILO: Integrate instructional aids into the lesson plan to maintain a logical flow and ensure that they support the learning objectives.
TC: Lesson Plan Integration & Logical Flow- Key strategies for integrating instructional aids into the lesson plan:1. Align visual aids with the lesson’s learning objectives and key takeaways.2. Use a consistent and coherent structure for the entire lesson.3. Ensure that each visual aid is introduced at the appropriate time and in the right context.- Practical exercises:1. Develop a lesson plan that includes the use of boards, slides, or props.2. Present the lesson plan to the class, demonstrating how the visual aids will be used.3. Discuss and refine the integration of visual aids based on peer and instructor feedback.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of instructional aids in enhancing student understanding and engagement, and make necessary adjustments to improve their impact.
TC: Evaluation & Improvement of Instructional Aids- Key strategies for evaluating the effectiveness of instructional aids:1. Collect feedback from students on the clarity and usefulness of the visual aids.2. Assess whether the visual aids helped to achieve the learning objectives.3. Identify areas where the visual aids could be improved or enhanced.- Practical exercises:1. Conduct a survey or focus group to gather student feedback on the visual aids.2. Analyze the feedback and identify common themes or issues.3. Revise the visual aids based on the feedback and re-evaluate their effectiveness in a subsequent lesson.

ILO: Break down the project timeline into smaller, manageable tasks and milestones, ensuring each team member understands their responsibilities. Transferable Skills: Time Management, Task Delegation
TC: Project Timeline Scaffolding- Breakdown of Project Phases: Guide students to divide the project into phases (e.g., research, design, implementation, testing).- Milestone Setting: Identify key milestones for each phase (e.g., “Complete user interviews by Week 2,” “Prototype ready by Week 4”).- Task Assignment: Use a Gantt chart or similar tool to assign specific tasks to team members with clear deadlines.

ILO: Develop a detailed project budget that includes all necessary resources and expenses, ensuring it aligns with the overall project goals. Transferable Skills: Financial Planning, Budgeting
TC: Project Budget Creation- Budget Categories: Introduce categories such as equipment, software, travel, and personnel.- Cost Estimation: Teach students how to estimate costs for each category (e.g., “AI sorting bin prototype: $500,” “Travel to local buildings: $100”).- Budget Justification: Ensure students can justify each expense in the context of the project’s objectives (e.g., “Travel is necessary for on-site testing and feedback collection”).

ILO: Create a comprehensive risk management plan that identifies potential project risks and outlines mitigation strategies. Transferable Skills: Risk Assessment, Problem Solving
TC: Risk Management Plan- Risk Identification: Guide students to brainstorm potential risks (e.g., “Delays in AI model training,” “Resistance from community members”).- Impact and Likelihood Assessment: Teach students to evaluate the impact and likelihood of each risk using a risk matrix.- Mitigation Strategies: Develop strategies to mitigate identified risks (e.g., “Regularly update the AI model to avoid delays,” “Conduct community engagement sessions to address concerns”).- Contingency Plans: Create contingency plans for high-impact, high-likelihood risks (e.g., “If AI model training is delayed, use a pre-trained model as a fallback”)

ILO: Craft a narrative that effectively communicates the project's purpose and impact, engaging the audience with a compelling story rather than just presenting a list of facts.
TC: Narrative Storytelling Workshop- Step 1: Introduction to Narrative Storytelling. Discuss the importance of storytelling in conveying project information and engage students in a brief exercise to identify key elements of a compelling story (e.g., setting, characters, conflict, resolution).- Step 2: Storyboard Creation. Students create a storyboard for their project, outlining the key points they want to communicate and how they will structure these points into a narrative. Instructor provides feedback on the structure and flow.- Step 3: Peer Review. Students share their storyboards with peers, who provide feedback on the clarity and engagement of the narrative. The instructor facilitates a discussion on common challenges and best practices.

ILO: Develop the ability to integrate data and factual information into a narrative, making the story both informative and emotionally resonant.
TC: Data-Driven Storytelling- Step 1: Data Collection and Analysis. Students gather and analyze relevant data related to their project, identifying key insights and trends.- Step 2: Integrating Data into the Narrative. Students learn techniques for integrating data into their narrative, such as using anecdotes, case studies, and visualizations. They practice embedding data points into their storyboards.- Step 3: Presentation and Feedback. Students present their data-driven narratives to the class. Peers and the instructor provide feedback on the effectiveness of the integration and the overall impact of the story.

ILO: Apply narrative storytelling techniques to create a cohesive and engaging final presentation, ensuring that the audience is both informed and inspired.
TC: Final Presentation Preparation- Step 1: Drafting the Final Presentation. Students draft their final presentation, incorporating the narrative storytelling techniques learned in previous sessions. They focus on creating a clear and engaging storyline that highlights the project's purpose, process, and impact.- Step 2: Rehearsal and Refinement. Students rehearse their presentations, focusing on delivery, timing, and audience engagement. Peers and the instructor provide constructive feedback to help refine the presentation.- Step 3: Final Presentation. Students deliver their final presentations to the class, showcasing their ability to tell a compelling story about their project. The instructor and peers evaluate the presentations based on the clarity, engagement, and effectiveness of the narrative.

ILO: Collaborate effectively with team members to identify and categorize project issues found during testing, and propose potential solutions. Transferable Skills: Teamwork, Problem Identification, Solution Generation
TC: Identify and Categorize Project Issues Teach students how to systematically identify and categorize issues found during the testing phase. This includes creating a structured issue log, categorizing issues by type (e.g., UI/UX, performance, security), and prioritizing them based on severity. Guide students in a group activity where they practice identifying and categorizing issues from a sample project, then discuss and propose potential solutions as a team.

ILO: Work collaboratively with team members to debug and resolve specific project issues, using appropriate tools and techniques. Transferable Skills: Debugging, Tool Proficiency, Collaboration
TC: Debugging Techniques and Tools Introduce students to common debugging tools and techniques, such as using logs, breakpoints, and unit tests. Provide hands-on practice with these tools through a series of guided exercises. Organize a group activity where students work together to debug a set of predefined issues in a project, ensuring each team member contributes and learns from the process.

ILO: Optimize project performance by collaboratively analyzing and implementing improvements based on testing feedback. Transferable Skills: Performance Optimization, Data Analysis, Collaborative Decision-Making
TC: Performance Optimization Strategies Teach students how to analyze testing feedback to identify areas for performance optimization. This includes using profiling tools to measure performance, identifying bottlenecks, and implementing optimizations. Conduct a group activity where students analyze performance data from a sample project, discuss potential optimizations, and implement changes as a team. Emphasize the importance of collaborative decision-making and iterative improvement.

ILO: Be able to identify and categorize potential project risks, including technical, financial, and human resource-related risks.
TC: Risk Identification and Categorization- Introduce the concept of risk management in projects.- Provide examples of different types of risks (technical, financial, human resources).- Guide students through a brainstorming session to identify potential risks in their project.- Use a risk matrix to categorize identified risks based on likelihood and impact.

ILO: Develop preliminary prevention plans for identified risks, including contingency measures and mitigation strategies.
TC: Preliminary Prevention Plans- Explain the importance of prevention plans in risk management.- Discuss common prevention strategies for different types of risks (e.g., regular code reviews for technical risks, budget tracking for financial risks, team-building activities for human resource risks).- Have students work in groups to develop specific prevention plans for the risks they identified.- Review and provide feedback on the prevention plans to ensure they are feasible and effective.

ILO: Formulate solution plans for potential risks, detailing steps to be taken if the risks materialize, and align these plans with the overall project objectives.
TC: Solution Plans and Alignment- Introduce the concept of contingency planning and its role in risk management.- Provide templates for creating solution plans, including steps to be taken, responsible parties, and timelines.- Have students create detailed solution plans for the identified risks, ensuring they include specific actions and responsible team members.- Ensure that the solution plans are aligned with the overall project objectives and discuss how they support the project’s success.

ILO: Be able to write a clear and concise problem statement in English and Chinese, identifying the key issues and objectives of the project. Transferable Skills: Problem Definition, Bilingual Communication
TC: Problem Statement Development: - Define the Problem: Identify and articulate the core issue or challenge that the project aims to address. - Objectives and Goals: Clearly state the project’s objectives and goals, ensuring they are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART). - Bilingual Writing: Write the problem statement in both English and Chinese, ensuring clarity and consistency in both languages.

ILO: Be able to develop a detailed and logical project timeline, including key milestones and deliverables, in both English and Chinese. Transferable Skills: Project Scheduling, Bilingual Documentation
TC: Project Timeline Creation: - Milestone Identification: List all key milestones and deliverables for the project, ensuring they align with the project objectives. - Timeline Development: Create a detailed Gantt chart or similar timeline, showing the sequence of activities, dependencies, and deadlines. - Bilingual Documentation: Document the project timeline in both English and Chinese, ensuring that both versions are accurate and consistent.

ILO: Be able to create a comprehensive budget and resource plan for the project, detailing all necessary resources and costs, in both English and Chinese. Transferable Skills: Budgeting, Resource Management, Bilingual Documentation
TC: Budget and Resource Planning: - Resource Identification: Identify all necessary resources, including personnel, materials, and equipment, required for the project. - Cost Estimation: Estimate the cost for each resource, including any external services or partnerships. - Budget Development: Create a detailed budget, including all estimated costs, and ensure it is aligned with the project timeline and objectives. - Bilingual Documentation: Document the budget and resource plan in both English and Chinese, ensuring that both versions are accurate and consistent.

ILO: Collect and analyze user feedback to identify areas for improvement in the project, and propose specific, actionable optimization suggestions.
TC: User Feedback Collection & Analysis: 1. Teach students how to design and distribute surveys or conduct interviews to gather user feedback. 2. Guide students through the process of analyzing qualitative and quantitative feedback data to identify common issues and pain points. 3. Instruct students on how to synthesize this feedback into a structured report, highlighting key areas that need improvement. 4. Facilitate a group discussion where students present their findings and collaboratively brainstorm targeted optimization suggestions.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of project features based on user feedback and make evidence-based recommendations for enhancement.
TC: Feature Evaluation & Enhancement: 1. Provide students with real-world examples of user feedback and the corresponding project features. 2. Teach students how to use metrics and KPIs to measure the performance of specific project features. 3. Guide students in creating a rubric to evaluate the effectiveness of each feature based on user feedback. 4. Have students present their evaluations and recommendations for feature enhancements, supported by data and user insights.

ILO: Develop a continuous improvement plan based on user feedback, including timelines and responsible team members, to ensure ongoing project optimization.
TC: Continuous Improvement Plan Development: 1. Introduce the concept of continuous improvement and its importance in project management. 2. Teach students how to create a detailed improvement plan, including setting clear goals, timelines, and assigning responsibilities. 3. Guide students in using tools like Gantt charts or project management software to visualize and track the improvement plan. 4. Facilitate a workshop where students draft and present their continuous improvement plans, incorporating feedback from peers and instructors to refine their strategies.

ILO: Students will be able to create and iterate on project prototypes using tools like Figma and Axure, demonstrating proficiency in user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design.

Iterative Feedback: Facilitate peer reviews and instructor feedback sessions to refine and improve the prototypes.

ILO: Students will be able to use Figma and Axure to conduct user testing and incorporate feedback into their prototypes, enhancing the usability and functionality of their designs.
TC: User Testing Techniques: Teach students how to set up and conduct user testing, including creating test scenarios and gathering feedback. Incorporating Feedback: Guide students through the process of analyzing user feedback and making necessary adjustments to their prototypes. Continuous Improvement: Encourage iterative cycles of testing and refinement, emphasizing the importance of continuous improvement in design.

ILO: Students will be able to collaborate effectively in a team setting, using Figma and Axure to co-create and manage shared project prototypes, ensuring consistency and coherence in the final product.
TC: Collaborative Features: Demonstrate how to use collaborative features in Figma and Axure, such as real-time editing, comments, and version control. Team Collaboration Exercise: Assign a group project where students must work together to create a comprehensive prototype, dividing tasks and responsibilities. Review and Integration: Have regular check-ins to review progress, address any issues, and ensure that all parts of the prototype are integrated seamlessly.

ILO: Effectively communicate with tutors and team members to clearly articulate project goals, ensuring all team members have a shared understanding of the project orientation and requirements.
TC: Project Orientation & Requirement Clarification- Key strategies for effective communication:1. Conduct regular check-ins with tutors to confirm project direction and receive feedback.2. Use structured meetings (e.g., weekly syncs) to ensure all team members are aligned on project goals and requirements.3. Create a shared document (e.g., Google Doc) to outline and track project objectives, timelines, and responsibilities.4. Develop a clear and concise project brief that includes the project’s purpose, scope, and key deliverables.

ILO: Develop and maintain open lines of communication with tutors and team members to address any questions or concerns regarding project requirements and expectations.
TC: Open Communication & Problem Solving- Strategies for maintaining open communication:1. Establish a dedicated communication channel (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams) for real-time updates and discussions.2. Schedule regular one-on-one meetings with tutors to discuss progress, challenges, and next steps.3. Encourage team members to ask questions and share concerns in a supportive environment.4. Use collaborative tools (e.g., Trello, Asana) to track project tasks, deadlines, and responsible parties.5. Conduct post-meeting summaries to ensure everyone is on the same page and to document key decisions and action items.

ILO: Collaboratively create and refine a project plan that aligns with the confirmed project orientation and requirements, ensuring all team members are aware of their roles and responsibilities.
TC: Project Plan Development & Role Allocation- Steps for creating and refining the project plan:1. Organize a project kickoff meeting to review the confirmed project orientation and requirements.2. Break down the project into manageable tasks and sub-tasks, assigning each to specific team members.3. Use a Gantt chart or similar tool to visualize the project timeline and dependencies.4. Develop a detailed project plan that includes milestones, deadlines, and resource allocation.5. Regularly review and update the project plan to reflect any changes in project scope or requirements.6. Ensure all team members understand their roles and responsibilities by creating a role-responsibility matrix and sharing it with the team.

ILO: Understand and apply basic data sorting and filtering techniques in Excel or WPS Spreadsheet to organize research data.
TC: Introduction to Data Sorting and Filtering- Explain the importance of data organization in research.- Demonstrate how to use basic sorting (A-Z, Z-A) and filtering (e.g., by value, by condition) in Excel or WPS Spreadsheet.- Provide a dataset for students to practice sorting and filtering.- Conduct a Q&A session to address any questions or issues.

ILO: Use advanced data analysis functions in Excel or WPS Spreadsheet, such as pivot tables and conditional formatting, to analyze and visualize research data.
TC: Advanced Data Analysis Techniques- Introduce pivot tables and their utility in summarizing and analyzing large datasets.- Show how to create and customize pivot tables in Excel or WPS Spreadsheet.- Explain conditional formatting and demonstrate its use in highlighting key data points.- Provide a dataset for students to practice creating pivot tables and applying conditional formatting.- Review and discuss the results with the class.

ILO: Apply data validation and error checking methods in Excel or WPS Spreadsheet to ensure the accuracy and reliability of research data.
TC: Data Validation and Error Checking- Discuss the importance of data validation and error checking in maintaining data integrity.- Demonstrate how to use data validation rules (e.g., list, date, number range) in Excel or WPS Spreadsheet.- Show how to use error checking tools (e.g., formula auditing, trace errors) to identify and correct mistakes.- Provide a dataset with intentional errors for students to practice validating and error checking.- Review and discuss the results with the class.

ILO: Understand the fundamental concepts and services of Alibaba Cloud, including Elastic Compute Service (ECS), Object Storage Service (OSS), and Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).
TC: Introduction to Alibaba Cloud Services - Key Concepts and Services: 1. Overview of Alibaba Cloud and its ecosystem. 2. Detailed explanation of core services: ECS, OSS, and VPC. 3. Hands-on lab: Setting up an ECS instance, creating an OSS bucket, and configuring a VPC.

ILO: Deploy a simple web application on Alibaba Cloud using ECS and OSS, and configure domain name and SSL certificate for secure access.
TC: Deploying a Web Application on Alibaba Cloud - Practical Steps: 1. Setting up a basic LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP) stack on ECS. 2. Uploading and serving static files from OSS. 3. Configuring a custom domain name and setting up an SSL certificate using Alibaba Cloud's Certificate Management Service. 4. Hands-on lab: Deploying a sample web application, configuring the domain, and securing it with SSL.

ILO: Monitor and manage the deployed application using Alibaba Cloud's monitoring and management tools, such as Cloud Monitor and Operation Orchestration Service (OOS).
TC: Monitoring and Managing Applications on Alibaba Cloud - Tools and Best Practices: 1. Introduction to Cloud Monitor and its features for real-time monitoring. 2. Setting up alerts and notifications for critical metrics. 3. Using OOS for automated operations and maintenance tasks. 4. Hands-on lab: Configuring Cloud Monitor, setting up alerts, and automating common tasks with OOS.

ILO: Understand the fundamental concepts of version control and its importance in managing project code and document versions.
TC: Introduction to Version Control- Key Concepts:1. Explain the basics of version control, including its purpose and benefits.2. Introduce Git as a popular version control tool and its role in collaborative projects.- Importance of Version Control:1. Discuss real-world scenarios where version control is crucial (e.g., tracking changes, resolving conflicts, maintaining history).2. Highlight the impact of version control on project management and team collaboration.

ILO: Learn how to set up and configure a Git repository for a project, including creating branches and committing changes.
TC: Setting Up and Configuring Git- Repository Setup:1. Guide students through the process of initializing a Git repository locally.2. Teach how to connect the local repository to a remote repository (e.g., GitHub, GitLab).- Branching and Committing:1. Demonstrate how to create and switch between branches.2. Show how to stage, commit, and push changes to the remote repository.3. Discuss best practices for writing meaningful commit messages.

ILO: Master the use of Git for managing project code and document versions, including merging branches, resolving conflicts, and using tags.

Discuss strategies for branch management, including feature branches and release branches.3. Demonstrate how to use Git for versioning and releasing project code and documents.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to assess and adjust project timelines based on real-time feedback and evolving project requirements

ILO: Effectively communicate and document project updates and changes to all stakeholders, ensuring transparency and alignment

The presentation should cover the key points from the report and address any questions or concerns from the audience. Instructor feedback focuses on clarity, completeness, and engagement.

ILO: Develop and implement a flexible project management plan that allows for continuous improvement and adaptation to changing circumstances
TC: Flexible Project Management Plan Development- Step 1: Plan Creation. Groups participate in a simulation exercise where they are presented with a series of unexpected events (e.g., resource constraints, team member unavailability). ILO: Understand and apply systematic methods for organizing and sorting project data, documents, and results to create a coherent and comprehensive project conclusion report.

ILO: Be able to organize regular team meetings and use meeting minutes tools to record key points and task assignments. Transferable Skills: Team Collaboration (sub-skill: meeting organization and documentation)

ILO: Students will be able to create a professional and visually appealing roadshow PPT using presentation tools like PowerPoint or Keynote, incorporating key elements such as a clear agenda, engaging visuals, and concise content. ILO: Effectively demonstrate and explain the project prototype to a diverse audience, highlighting key design ideas and functional points.

TC: 1) Documentation Workshop: Students will participate in a workshop on creating high-quality project documentation. The workshop will cover: a. Tools and templates for creating professional-looking documents. 2) Drafting and Review: Students will draft their project documentation and submit it for peer and instructor review. 3) Finalization: Based on the feedback received, students will finalize their documentation, ensuring it is clear, comprehensive, and user-friendly. 4) Presentation: Students will present their finalized documentation to the class, explaining the key sections and how they support the project's goals.

ILO: Effectively listen to and respond to questions and suggestions from judges or audiences during roadshows, demonstrating clear understanding and adaptability.

Provide concise, relevant, and clear answers, avoiding jargon or overly technical language.

ILO: Adapt and refine project presentations based on feedback received from judges or audiences during roadshows, ensuring alignment with project goals and stakeholder needs.

Revise the content to better align with the project’s objectives and stakeholder needs.2. Adjust the visual aids and slides to enhance clarity and engagement.3. Rehearse the revised presentation to ensure smooth delivery.4. Seek additional feedback from peers or mentors to validate the changes.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to handle unexpected questions or challenging scenarios during roadshows, maintaining composure and providing thoughtful, well-reasoned responses.

Develop a list of common challenging scenarios and prepare responses.3. Practice responding to unexpected questions in mock sessions with peers or mentors.- Techniques for handling challenging scenarios:1. Stay calm and composed, taking a moment to think before responding.2. Use the 3C (Clarify, Consider, Conclude) method to structure your response: Clarify the question, consider the implications, and conclude with a well-reasoned answer.3. If unsure, acknowledge the complexity of the question and offer to follow up with more information.4. Use storytelling or examples to illustrate your points and make the response more relatable.

TC: Project Roadshow Presentation Development - Step 1: Structuring the Presentation. Guide students on how to structure their presentation (introduction, problem statement, solution, methodology, impact, and conclusion). - Step 2: Crafting the Narrative. Teach students how to create a compelling narrative that engages the audience and highlights the key points of the project. - Step 3: Visual Aids and Design. Provide guidance on creating effective visual aids (slides, charts, images) and ensuring the design is consistent and professional. - Step 4: Practice and Feedback. Allow students to practice their presentations and provide constructive feedback to improve delivery and clarity.

ILO: Effectively handle Q&A sessions during the project roadshow, demonstrating the ability to think on one's feet and provide clear, concise, and relevant responses. Transferable Skills: Critical Thinking, On-the-Spot Problem Solving, Communication
TC: Q&A Session Preparation and Handling - Step 1: Anticipating Questions. Help students anticipate common and challenging questions that might arise during the Q&A session. - Step 2: Preparing Responses. Guide students in preparing clear, concise, and well-structured responses to these anticipated questions. - Step 3: Mock Q&A Sessions. Conduct mock Q&A sessions where students can practice answering questions and receive feedback on their responses. - Step 4: Techniques for Effective Q&A. Teach techniques such as active listening, pausing before answering, and redirecting irrelevant or off-topic questions.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to adapt the project roadshow presentation to different audiences, tailoring the content and delivery to meet the specific needs and interests of each group. Transferable Skills: Audience Analysis, Adaptability, Persuasive Communication
TC: Tailoring Presentations for Different Audiences - Step 1: Audience Analysis. Teach students how to analyze their audience (e.g., stakeholders, investors, community members) and understand their needs and interests. - Step 2: Customizing Content. Guide students in customizing the content of their presentation to address the specific concerns and interests of each audience. - Step 3: Adjusting Delivery. Provide tips on adjusting the delivery style (e.g., tone, pace, level of detail) to suit different audiences. - Step 4: Role-Playing Exercises. Conduct role-playing exercises where students present to different simulated audiences and receive feedback on their ability to tailor the presentation effectively.

ILO: Understand the principles of questionnaire design and apply them to create a scientifically sound and user-friendly survey using tools like Wenjuanxing or Google Forms.
TC: Principles of Questionnaire Design- Step 1: Introduction to Questionnaire Design (15 mins)Discuss the importance of clear, concise, and unbiased questions.- Step 2: Best Practices for Questionnaire Design (20 mins)Explore examples of good and bad questionnaires, and discuss best practices for creating effective surveys.- Step 3: Hands-on Practice (30 mins)Students will use Wenjuanxing or Google Forms to create a sample questionnaire based on a given topic.

ILO: Develop the ability to identify and address potential biases in questionnaires to ensure the collection of accurate and reliable data.
TC: Identifying and Addressing Biases in Questionnaires- Step 1: Understanding Types of Bias (15 mins)Introduce common types of bias in surveys, such as leading questions, loaded language, and order effects.- Step 2: Case Studies (20 mins)Analyze real-world examples of biased questionnaires and discuss how they can be improved.- Step 3: Peer Review (25 mins)Students will review each other's questionnaires, identifying and addressing any biases found.

ILO: Learn to analyze and interpret the data collected from questionnaires to extract meaningful insights and inform project decisions.
TC: Analyzing and Interpreting Data from Questionnaires- Step 1: Data Collection and Preparation (15 mins)Guide students through the process of collecting and preparing data from their questionnaires for analysis.- Step 2: Data Analysis Techniques (20 mins)Teach basic data analysis techniques, such as frequency distributions, cross-tabulations, and simple statistical tests.- Step 3: Extracting Insights (25 mins)Students will work in groups to analyze their data, extract key insights, and present their findings to the class.

ILO: Be able to design and conduct in-depth one-on-one interviews with target users, accurately recording key information and insights.
TC: Interview Design and Conduct: 1. Introduction to Effective Interviewing (10 mins): Discuss the importance of open-ended questions, active listening, and note-taking. 2. Role-Play Exercise (30 mins): Students practice conducting a one-on-one interview with a peer, focusing on gathering detailed and accurate information. 3. Debrief and Feedback (15 mins): Review the role-play exercises, discuss common challenges, and provide feedback on how to improve interviewing techniques.

ILO: Be able to design and conduct in-depth group interviews with target users, accurately recording key information and insights.
TC: Group Interview Design and Conduct: 1. Group Interview Techniques (10 mins): Introduce strategies for managing group dynamics, ensuring all participants are heard, and capturing diverse perspectives. 2. Group Interview Simulation (40 mins): Students form small groups and practice conducting a group interview, with each student taking turns as the interviewer and participant. 3. Reflection and Analysis (15 mins): Discuss the experience, identify strengths and areas for improvement, and share best practices for recording and synthesizing group interview data.

ILO: Be able to analyze and synthesize data from multiple interviews, identifying key themes and insights that can inform project development.
TC: Data Analysis and Synthesis: 1. Introduction to Data Analysis (10 mins): Explain the process of coding and categorizing qualitative data, and the importance of triangulating information. 2. Data Synthesis Workshop (30 mins): Students work in pairs or small groups to analyze and synthesize data from their one-on-one and group interviews, identifying common themes and insights. 3. Presentation and Discussion (20 mins): Each group presents their findings, and the class discusses the implications for project development, highlighting the most significant insights and potential next steps.

ILO: Effectively sort and categorize questionnaire data to identify key user needs and preferences, ensuring the data is organized in a manner that facilitates further analysis.
TC: Data Sorting & Categorization- Step 1: Data Collection (30 mins)Students gather and review all questionnaire data.- Step 2: Data Categorization (45 mins)Students use a structured approach to sort the data into categories based on themes or user segments. Tools like Excel or Google Sheets can be used for this purpose.- Step 3: Verification (15 mins)Students cross-check their categorized data with peers to ensure accuracy and completeness.

ILO: Analyze interview records to extract meaningful insights and patterns, distinguishing between explicit and implicit user demands, and synthesizing this information into actionable recommendations.
TC: Interview Analysis & Synthesis- Step 1: Transcription & Review (60 mins)Students transcribe and review the interview records, noting key points and observations.- Step 2: Identifying Patterns (45 mins)Students identify common themes and patterns in the interview data, using techniques such as thematic analysis.- Step 3: Synthesizing Insights (30 mins)Students synthesize the identified patterns into actionable recommendations, distinguishing between explicit and implicit user demands. This can be done through a group discussion or a written report.

ILO: Integrate findings from both questionnaire data and interview records to create a comprehensive user demand profile, highlighting the most critical user needs and preferences.
TC: Integration of Findings & Profile Creation- Step 1: Data Integration (45 mins)Students combine the sorted questionnaire data and analyzed interview records into a single, cohesive dataset.- Step 2: Creating User Demand Profile (60 mins)Students develop a detailed user demand profile, summarizing the most critical user needs and preferences. The profile should include visual aids like charts and graphs to illustrate key findings.- Step 3: Peer Review (30 mins)Students present their user demand profiles to their peers for feedback and validation, ensuring the profiles are clear, comprehensive, and actionable.

ILO: Analyze survey data to identify key user characteristics and preferences, and create a detailed user portrait that informs project design and optimization.
TC: Survey Data Analysis & User Portrait Creation - Step 1: Data Collection. Review the survey results, focusing on demographic, behavioral, and preference data. - Step 2: Data Analysis. Use statistical tools (e.g., Excel, SPSS) to analyze the data, identifying patterns and trends. - Step 3: User Portrait Development. Based on the analysis, create a detailed user portrait that includes key characteristics, preferences, and pain points. - Step 4: Application to Project Design. Discuss how the user portrait can inform the project's design and optimization, ensuring it aligns with user needs and expectations.

ILO: Synthesize user feedback and survey data to refine user portraits and ensure they accurately reflect the target audience for the project.
TC: Refining User Portraits with Feedback - Step 1: Collect User Feedback. Gather additional feedback from users through interviews or focus groups. - Step 2: Integrate Feedback. Incorporate the new feedback into the existing user portraits, updating and refining them as necessary. - Step 3: Validate User Portraits. Conduct a validation session with a small group of users to ensure the updated portraits accurately represent their characteristics and preferences. - Step 4: Finalize User Portraits. Finalize the user portraits, making any necessary adjustments based on the validation session, and document the process and findings.

ILO: Use user portraits to guide the development of project features and solutions, ensuring they are tailored to meet the specific needs and preferences of the target audience.
TC: User-Centered Project Development - Step 1: Feature Brainstorming. Use the user portraits to brainstorm project features and solutions that address the identified needs and preferences. - Step 2: Prioritize Features. Rank the proposed features based on their alignment with user needs and the project’s objectives. - Step 3: Prototype Development. Develop prototypes of the top-priority features, incorporating user-centered design principles. - Step 4: User Testing. Conduct user testing sessions to gather feedback on the prototypes, and use this feedback to iterate and improve the features. - Step 5: Finalize Features. Finalize the project features, ensuring they are well-aligned with the user portraits and ready for implementation.

ILO: Develop the ability to write a clear and concise project summary report that effectively communicates the key findings, outcomes, and next steps of the project.
TC: - Step 1: Project Summary Report Template. Introduce a structured template for writing a project summary report, including sections such as: 1) Executive Summary, 2) Project Objectives, 3) Key Findings, 4) Outcomes, 5) Next Steps, and 6) Appendices.\n- Step 2: Writing Workshop. Conduct a workshop where students practice writing each section of the project summary report using their own project data. Provide feedback on clarity, conciseness, and coherence.\n- Step 3: Peer Review. Have students exchange their draft reports with peers for feedback. Focus on ensuring that the key points are clearly communicated and that the report is well-organized.

ILO: Organize and present project materials in a logical and accessible manner, suitable for future reference and reuse by the team and stakeholders.
TC: - Step 1: Organizing Project Materials. Teach students how to organize project materials into a logical and accessible structure, using tools like Feishu Drive or Google Drive. Emphasize the importance of categorization (e.g., by type, date, or phase).\n- Step 2: Creating a Project Repository. Guide students in setting up a shared repository for all project materials, including documents, meeting notes, and research findings. Ensure that the repository is easy to navigate and includes a clear directory structure.\n- Step 3: Best Practices for Documentation. Discuss best practices for documenting project materials, such as using consistent naming conventions, version control, and metadata tagging. Provide examples and templates for different types of documents.

ILO: Evaluate and refine the project summary and organized materials to ensure they meet the standards of clarity, completeness, and relevance for the intended audience.
TC: - Step 1: Evaluation Criteria. Introduce a set of evaluation criteria for assessing the quality of the project summary and organized materials. These criteria should include: 1) Clarity, 2) Completeness, 3) Relevance, 4) Accessibility, and 5) Professionalism.\n- Step 2: Self-Assessment. Have students use the evaluation criteria to self-assess their project summary and organized materials. Encourage them to identify areas for improvement and make necessary revisions.\n- Step 3: Instructor and Peer Feedback. Provide detailed feedback on the project summary and organized materials, focusing on the evaluation criteria. Facilitate a peer review session where students can provide constructive feedback to each other, emphasizing the need for clarity, completeness, and relevance.

ILO: Apply the Define-Ideate-Prototype framework to identify and solve a real-world problem from a user-centric perspective.
TC: Introduction to Design Thinking: \\- Lecture on the Define-Ideate-Prototype framework, emphasizing the importance of user-centric design. \\- Case study analysis: Students will analyze a successful real-world application of the Define-Ideate-Prototype framework. \\- Group Activity: Each group selects a real-world problem and applies the Define stage to clearly define the problem and user needs.

ILO: Generate and evaluate multiple solutions for a defined real-world problem using ideation techniques.
TC: Ideation Techniques and Solution Generation: \\- Workshop on various ideation techniques (e.g., brainstorming, SCAMPER, mind mapping). \\- Group Activity: Using the problem defined in the previous session, students generate a wide range of potential solutions. \\- Peer Review: Groups present their top 3-5 solutions, and peers provide feedback based on feasibility, creativity, and alignment with user needs. \\- Instructor Feedback: Provide targeted feedback on the ideation process and the quality of the generated solutions.

ILO: Develop and test a prototype to validate the most promising solution, and iterate based on user feedback.
TC: Prototyping and User Testing: \\- Lecture on prototyping methods and tools, including low-fidelity and high-ffidelity prototypes. \\- Group Activity: Each group develops a prototype of their most promising solution. \\- User Testing: Groups conduct user testing sessions to gather feedback on the prototype. \\- Iteration: Based on user feedback, groups refine and iterate on their prototype. \\- Final Presentation: Each group presents their final prototype and the iterative process, highlighting how user feedback was incorporated.

ILO: Analyze and decompose a project vision into specific, actionable user stories and development tasks. Transferable Skills: Backlog Refinement, User Story Writing, Task Decomposition
TC: Project Vision Decomposition & User Story Creation: Start with a high-level project vision (e.g., 'Develop a mobile app for community waste management'). Break down the vision into smaller, manageable user stories and development tasks. Use the INVEST criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) to ensure each user story is well-defined. Create a backlog of these user stories and tasks, prioritizing them based on value and effort.

ILO: Refine and prioritize the backlog of user stories and tasks to ensure they are clear, feasible, and aligned with the project goals. Transferable Skills: Backlog Management, Prioritization, Stakeholder Communication
TC: Backlog Refinement & Prioritization: Conduct a backlog refinement session where the team reviews and refines the initial backlog. Ensure that each user story and task is clear, feasible, and aligned with the project goals. Use techniques such as MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have) or the Kano Model to prioritize the backlog. Engage with stakeholders to validate the priorities and make any necessary adjustments.

ILO: Create and maintain a detailed project roadmap that includes milestones, deadlines, and dependencies for the refined backlog. Transferable Skills: Project Planning, Roadmap Development, Dependency Management
TC: Project Roadmap Development: Develop a detailed project roadmap based on the refined and prioritized backlog. Identify key milestones, set realistic deadlines, and map out dependencies between tasks. Use tools like Gantt charts or Kanban boards to visualize the roadmap. Regularly update the roadmap as the project progresses and communicate changes to the team and stakeholders.

ILO: Critically analyze and reflect on the successes and failures of the project, identifying key lessons learned to inform future projects. Transferable Skills: Critical thinking, self-reflection
TC: Structured Reflection Framework Introduce a structured reflection framework that guides students through the process of analyzing project outcomes. Key components include: Identifying what went well (successes) and what didn’t (failures). Exploring the reasons behind these outcomes. Extracting actionable insights and lessons learned. Developing a plan for applying these lessons in future projects.

ILO: Develop a comprehensive post-project report that synthesizes the project's key findings, challenges, and recommendations for improvement. Transferable Skills: Written communication, strategic planning
TC: Post-Project Report Template Provide a detailed template for the post-project report, including: Executive Summary: A brief overview of the project and its outcomes. Project Overview: Description of the project, objectives, and methods. Key Findings: Detailed analysis of the project's results, including both successes and failures. Challenges: Identification and discussion of the main challenges faced. Recommendations: Actionable suggestions for improvement based on the lessons learned. Conclusion: Summary of the key takeaways and future directions.

ILO: Facilitate a peer review session where students present their reflections and receive feedback from their peers to refine their insights and improve future project planning. Transferable Skills: Peer feedback, collaborative learning
TC: Peer Review Session Organize a peer review session where students present their reflections and receive constructive feedback. Structure the session as follows: Presentation: Each student presents their reflection, focusing on key lessons learned and proposed improvements. Feedback: Peers provide feedback using a structured feedback form, covering areas such as clarity of reflection, depth of analysis, and feasibility of proposed improvements. Discussion: Facilitate a group discussion to explore common themes and insights. Follow-Up: Students revise their reflections based on the feedback received and submit a final version.

ILO: Independently synthesize and apply knowledge from academic papers and GitHub source code to master a new technology without relying on traditional textbooks.
