TC: Self-Directed Learning Workshop: Introduction to New Technologies- Research and Synthesis: Students are provided with a list of academic papers and links to relevant GitHub repositories. They must read and analyze these resources to understand the key concepts and functionalities of the new technology.- Practical Application: Students will implement a small project or feature using the new technology, demonstrating their understanding and ability to apply the knowledge gained from the research and synthesis phase.

ILO: Develop a structured learning plan for mastering a new technology, including milestones and self-assessment criteria.
TC: Structured Learning Plan Development- Planning Session: Students will create a detailed learning plan that includes specific milestones, deadlines, and self-assessment criteria. The plan should outline how they will use academic papers and GitHub source code to learn the new technology.- Milestone Setting: Students will set clear, achievable milestones (e.g., understanding the core concepts by Week 1, implementing a basic feature by Week 2).- Self-Assessment: Students will define criteria for self-assessment at each milestone, such as successfully running a sample code or passing a self-created quiz based on the academic papers.

ILO: Effectively communicate and document the process of learning and applying a new technology, including challenges and solutions encountered.
TC: Learning Journal and Presentation- Learning Journal: Students will maintain a learning journal throughout the process, documenting their progress, challenges, and solutions. This journal should include references to specific academic papers and GitHub repositories used, as well as any code snippets or diagrams created during the learning process.- Final Presentation: At the end of the learning period, students will present their journey, including the technologies learned, the methods used, and the projects implemented. They will also discuss the challenges they faced and the solutions they found, providing insights for future learners.

ILO: Apply Non-Violent Communication (NVC) techniques to resolve internal team conflicts effectively during high-pressure project phases.
TC: Conflict Resolution Workshop - NVC Techniques: \\- Step 1: Introduction to NVC. Explain the four components of NVC: Observation, Feeling, Need, and Request (OFNR). \\- Step 2: Role-Playing Scenarios. Students practice NVC in simulated high-pressure conflict scenarios, such as missed deadlines or task misalignment. \\- Step 3: Peer Feedback. Peers provide feedback on the effectiveness of NVC techniques used, focusing on clarity, empathy, and constructive resolution. \\- Step 4: Instructor Feedback. Provide targeted feedback on NVC application, highlighting areas for improvement and reinforcing best practices.

ILO: Identify and address the underlying needs and emotions of team members during conflicts using NVC, fostering a more collaborative and supportive team environment.
TC: Emotional Intelligence and Needs Identification - NVC Training: \\- Step 1: Understanding Emotions. Discuss common emotions experienced during conflicts and their impact on communication. \\- Step 2: Identifying Needs. Guide students to identify and articulate the underlying needs of team members in conflict situations. \\- Step 3: Group Discussion. Students share personal experiences and discuss how NVC can be applied to address these needs. \\- Step 4: Case Studies. Analyze real-world case studies where NVC was successfully used to resolve team conflicts, focusing on the identification and addressing of needs.

ILO: Develop and implement a structured NVC-based conflict resolution plan for a given project phase, ensuring that all team members are heard and their concerns are addressed constructively.
TC: Structured Conflict Resolution Plan - NVC Implementation: \\- Step 1: Plan Development. Students create a detailed NVC-based conflict resolution plan for a specific project phase, including steps for observation, feeling, need, and request. \\- Step 2: Role-Playing Practice. Students role-play the implementation of the NVC plan in a high-pressure scenario, focusing on active listening and empathetic responses. \\- Step 3: Peer Review. Peers review the NVC plan and provide feedback on its clarity, feasibility, and effectiveness. \\- Step 4: Instructor Feedback. Provide feedback on the NVC plan, emphasizing the importance of clear communication, active listening, and constructive problem-solving.

ILO: Reframe a complex problem by challenging underlying assumptions and redefining the problem statement to identify new potential solutions. Transferable Skills: Critical Thinking, Problem Solving
TC: Problem Reframing Workshop - Step 1: Identify Assumptions (20 mins)Students will work in groups to list all the assumptions they have made about the problem. - Step 2: Challenge Assumptions (30 mins)Each group will present their assumptions, and the class will collectively challenge these assumptions. - Step 3: Redefine the Problem (40 mins)Using the insights from the previous steps, students will redefine the problem statement to open up new solution pathways.

ILO: Develop a structured approach to reframing problems by systematically breaking down the problem into its components and identifying areas for redefinition. Transferable Skills: Analytical Thinking, Systematic Problem Solving
TC: Structured Problem Reframing Activity - Step 1: Break Down the Problem (20 mins)Students will break down the problem into its key components using a provided template. - Step 2: Identify Critical Components (30 mins)Groups will identify which components are most critical to the problem and why. - Step 3: Redefine Components (40 mins)For each critical component, students will brainstorm alternative definitions or perspectives. - Step 4: Synthesize New Problem Statement (30 mins)Students will synthesize the new problem statement based on the redefined components.

ILO: Apply reframing techniques to a real-world problem by generating multiple alternative problem statements and evaluating their potential impact. Transferable Skills: Creative Problem Solving, Impact Assessment
TC: Real-World Problem Reframing Exercise - Step 1: Select a Real-World Problem (15 mins)Students will select a real-world problem from a provided list. - Step 2: Generate Alternative Problem Statements (40 mins)In groups, students will generate at least three alternative problem statements for the selected problem. - Step 3: Evaluate Potential Impact (40 mins)Each group will evaluate the potential impact of each alternative problem statement, considering feasibility, scalability, and alignment with the original problem. - Step 4: Present and Discuss (30 mins)Groups will present their alternative problem statements and evaluations to the class, followed by a discussion on the most promising options.

ILO: Identify and synthesize key insights from a variety of technical sources, such as academic papers, technical blogs, and documentation, to form a coherent understanding of a specific topic.
TC: Information Synthesis from Diverse Sources- Step 1: Source Selection (20 mins)Students select and review a range of sources, including academic papers, technical blogs, and documentation.- Step 2: Core Logic Extraction (30 mins)Students extract the main arguments, methodologies, and findings from each source, identifying the core logic and key insights.- Step 3: Synthesis and Integration (40 mins)Students integrate the extracted information into a coherent narrative, highlighting connections and common themes across the sources.

ILO: Develop a structured approach to organizing and presenting synthesized information, ensuring clarity and logical flow in the final output.
TC: Structured Presentation of Synthesized Information- Step 1: Outline Creation (20 mins)Students create an outline for their synthesis, organizing the key points and insights logically.- Step 2: Drafting (40 mins)Students draft the synthesis, using the outline to guide the structure and flow of the document. They ensure that each section builds on the previous one and contributes to the overall coherence.- Step 3: Review and Refinement (20 mins)Students review their draft, checking for clarity, logical flow, and coherence. They make necessary revisions to improve the presentation of the synthesized information.

ILO: Evaluate the quality and relevance of the synthesized information, ensuring it meets the criteria for academic rigor and practical application.
TC: Evaluation and Refinement of Synthesized Information- Step 1: Peer Review (20 mins)Students exchange their syntheses with peers for feedback on clarity, logical flow, and relevance.- Step 2: Self-Assessment (20 mins)Students self-assess their syntheses against a provided rubric, focusing on the quality and relevance of the information.- Step 3: Final Revisions (30 mins)Students incorporate feedback from peer reviews and self-assessments, making final revisions to ensure the synthesized information meets the required standards of academic rigor and practical application.

ILO: Effectively communicate and translate cross-domain concepts to facilitate understanding and collaboration between team members from diverse professional backgrounds (e.g., Education vs. Engineering). Transferable Skills: Cross-Domain Translation, Interpersonal & Collaborative Communication
TC: Cross-Domain Concept Translation - Introduce the importance of cross-domain translation in project teams. - Provide examples of common jargon and terminology used in different fields (e.g., educational theories, engineering principles). - Facilitate a workshop where students practice translating a technical document (e.g., an engineering report) into a version that is understandable for an education professional, and vice versa. - Use role-playing exercises to simulate real-world scenarios where cross-domain translation is necessary.

ILO: Develop strategies to align goals and expectations between team members with diverse professional backgrounds, ensuring a shared understanding and effective collaboration. Transferable Skills: Goal Alignment, Interpersonal & Collaborative Communication
TC: Goal Alignment Strategies - Discuss the importance of goal alignment in cross-disciplinary teams. - Teach techniques for setting and communicating clear, measurable, and achievable goals (e.g., SMART goals). - Conduct a group activity where students identify and align their individual goals with the overall project objectives. - Provide templates and tools for creating a shared vision and mission statement that reflects the collective goals of the team. - Facilitate a session on active listening and empathy to ensure that all team members feel heard and understood.

ILO: Facilitate effective communication and problem-solving within a cross-disciplinary team by acting as a linguistic bridge, ensuring that all team members are on the same page. Transferable Skills: Cross-Domain Translation, Problem-Solving, Interpersonal & Collaborative Communication
TC: Facilitating Cross-Disciplinary Communication - Introduce the role of a linguistic bridge in a cross-disciplinary team. - Provide case studies of successful cross-disciplinary projects and analyze how effective communication and translation played a key role. - Conduct a hands-on exercise where students are given a complex problem and must work together to solve it, with each student representing a different professional background (e.g., education, engineering, business). - Teach strategies for facilitating discussions, such as using visual aids, analogies, and plain language. - Role-play scenarios where students must resolve misunderstandings and conflicts arising from cross-disciplinary communication gaps.

ILO: Identify and analyze the needs and expectations of various stakeholders (mentors, university resources, and corporate partners) to ensure alignment and effective communication. Transferable Skills: Stakeholder Management (sub-skill: stakeholder analysis and communication)
TC: Stakeholder Analysis and Communication- Step 1: Introduction to Stakeholders. Define the roles and responsibilities of mentors, university resources, and corporate partners. Discuss the importance of aligning their expectations.- Step 2: Stakeholder Mapping. Use a stakeholder map to identify and categorize stakeholders based on their influence and interest in the project. Prioritize key stakeholders for more focused engagement.- Step 3: Communication Plan. Develop a communication plan that outlines how and when to engage with each stakeholder group. Include specific communication channels (e.g., email, meetings, project management tools) and frequency of updates.

ILO: Develop and implement a stakeholder engagement strategy that includes regular updates, feedback loops, and conflict resolution mechanisms. Transferable Skills: Stakeholder Management (sub-skill: stakeholder engagement and conflict resolution)
TC: Stakeholder Engagement and Conflict Resolution- Step 1: Engagement Strategy. Create a detailed stakeholder engagement strategy that includes regular check-ins, progress updates, and feedback sessions. Ensure that the strategy is tailored to the preferences and needs of each stakeholder group.- Step 2: Feedback Loops. Establish a system for collecting and incorporating feedback from stakeholders. This can include surveys, focus groups, or one-on-one meetings. Emphasize the importance of open and transparent communication.- Step 3: Conflict Resolution. Teach conflict resolution techniques and provide case studies or role-playing exercises to practice handling disagreements and conflicts. Discuss the importance of maintaining positive relationships and finding mutually beneficial solutions.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of stakeholder management strategies and make adjustments as needed to ensure continuous improvement. Transferable Skills: Stakeholder Management (sub-skill: continuous improvement and evaluation)
TC: Evaluation and Continuous Improvement- Step 1: Evaluation Metrics. Introduce key metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of stakeholder management strategies, such as stakeholder satisfaction, project progress, and communication quality.- Step 2: Data Collection. Teach methods for collecting data on these metrics, including surveys, interviews, and performance reviews. Provide templates and tools to facilitate this process.- Step 3: Continuous Improvement. Guide students through the process of analyzing the collected data and making informed adjustments to their stakeholder management strategies. Encourage a culture of continuous improvement and learning from both successes and challenges.

ILO: Utilize workflow visualization tools (e.g., Miro/Jira) to identify and analyze progress bottlenecks in project workflows.
TC: Bottleneck Analysis with Workflow Visualization Tools- Step 1: Introduction to Miro/Jira (30 mins). Teach students the basics of using Miro/Jira for workflow visualization, including creating boards, adding tasks, and setting up swimlanes.- Step 2: Workflow Mapping (45 mins). Students map out their current project workflows on Miro/Jira, identifying key stages and tasks.- Step 3: Bottleneck Identification (30 mins). Students use the visualized workflows to identify potential bottlenecks, such as delays, resource constraints, or task dependencies. Discuss and document these bottlenecks.

ILO: Adopt an iterative prototyping approach to deliver a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) by prioritizing rapid iteration and learning from failures.
TC: Iterative Prototyping and MVP Thinking- Step 1: Introduction to Iterative Prototyping (30 mins). Explain the principles of iterative prototyping, emphasizing the importance of rapid iteration and learning from failures.- Step 2: Defining the MVP (45 mins). Students define the core features and functionalities that constitute their MVP, focusing on the minimum set of features needed to test the concept.- Step 3: Prototyping and Testing (60 mins). Students create a basic prototype of their MVP and conduct initial testing, gathering feedback and identifying areas for improvement. Discuss the results and plan the next iteration.

ILO: Apply Agile/Scrum principles to structure project work, manage backlogs, and adapt to changes through regular sprints and standups.
TC: Agile/Scrum Principles for Project Management- Step 1: Core Concepts (45 mins). Teach key Agile/Scrum principles, including sprints, daily standups, backlog management, and sprint reviews. Emphasize the importance of flexibility and adaptability in project management.- Step 2: Backlog Management (30 mins). Students learn how to prioritize and manage their project backlogs, ensuring that tasks are aligned with project goals and timelines. Use Jira or Miro to create and manage the backlog.- Step 3: Sprint Planning and Execution (60 mins). Students plan and execute a 2-week sprint, breaking down tasks into manageable units and assigning them to team members. Conduct daily standups to discuss progress, address blockers, and adjust plans as needed. Review the sprint at the end to assess deliverables and plan the next sprint.

ILO: Accurately estimate the development cycles for project tasks and adjust sprint goals based on historical team velocity to ensure realistic and achievable timelines. Transferable Skills: Sprint Planning and Velocity Tracking (sub-skill: accurate estimation and goal adjustment)
TC: Sprint Planning and Velocity Tracking- Step 1: Historical Velocity Analysis. Review past sprints to calculate the average velocity of the team. Discuss the importance of velocity in planning.- Step 2: Task Estimation Workshop. Guide students through a detailed task breakdown, estimating the time required for each task using techniques like story points or hours. Use tools like Jira or Trello to visualize the sprint backlog.- Step 3: Sprint Goal Setting. Based on the estimated task times and historical velocity, set realistic sprint goals. Discuss how to adjust goals if the initial estimates are too optimistic or pessimistic.

ILO: Identify and track key performance indicators (KPIs) that reflect the team's progress and productivity, and use these KPIs to make data-driven decisions during sprint reviews. Transferable Skills: Data-Driven Decision Making (sub-skill: KPI tracking and analysis)
TC: KPI Tracking and Analysis- Step 1: KPI Selection. Introduce common KPIs for Agile projects, such as lead time, cycle time, and burndown rate. Discuss which KPIs are most relevant for the current project.- Step 2: KPI Monitoring Setup. Set up dashboards or reports in tools like Jira, Trello, or Google Sheets to track the selected KPIs. Ensure all team members have access and understand how to interpret the data.- Step 3: Sprint Review and KPI Analysis. During the sprint review, analyze the KPIs to assess the team's performance. Discuss any trends or anomalies and make data-driven decisions to improve future sprints.

ILO: Develop and implement a continuous improvement process for sprint planning and velocity tracking, incorporating feedback from retrospectives and adapting the process to better fit the team's needs. Transferable Skills: Continuous Improvement (sub-skill: process refinement and adaptation)
TC: Continuous Improvement Process- Step 1: Retrospective Feedback Collection. Conduct a retrospective meeting to gather feedback on the sprint planning and velocity tracking process. Use techniques like the Start, Stop, Continue method to identify areas for improvement.- Step 2: Process Refinement. Based on the feedback, refine the sprint planning and velocity tracking process. This might include adjusting estimation techniques, improving communication, or modifying the sprint review format.- Step 3: Implementation and Follow-Up. Implement the refined process in the next sprint and schedule a follow-up review to assess its effectiveness. Continuously iterate and adapt the process based on ongoing feedback and team dynamics.

ILO: Analyze and document the potential risks and uncertainties in a project, and develop strategies to mitigate these ambiguities. Transferable Skills: Risk Management (sub-skill: ambiguity tolerance)
TC: Risk and Uncertainty Analysis: Teams will use a structured risk assessment tool (e.g., SWOT analysis) to identify and document potential risks and uncertainties in their project. They will then develop mitigation strategies for each identified risk, including contingency plans and communication protocols. This will be documented in a shared Miro board or Google Doc.

ILO: Create a flexible project roadmap that can adapt to changing requirements and unknown technical paths, ensuring continuous progress. Transferable Skills: Project Management (sub-skill: adaptive planning)
TC: Adaptive Project Roadmap: Introduce a dynamic project roadmap template that allows for flexibility and adaptability. The template will include sections for high-level milestones, key deliverables, and a timeline with buffer periods. Teams will use this template to create a roadmap that can accommodate changes and uncertainties. Regular check-ins and adjustments will be scheduled to ensure the roadmap remains relevant and effective.

ILO: Develop a communication plan to keep all stakeholders informed and engaged, even when project details are ambiguous or evolving. Transferable Skills: Communication (sub-skill: stakeholder engagement)
TC: Stakeholder Communication Plan: Teams will create a comprehensive communication plan that outlines how they will keep stakeholders informed and engaged throughout the project. The plan will include regular updates (e.g., weekly newsletters, bi-weekly status meetings), channels of communication (e.g., email, Slack, Feishu), and a feedback mechanism to gather and incorporate stakeholder input. The plan will be presented to the class for peer review and instructor feedback.

ILO: Develop a clear and concise technical pitch that effectively communicates the value proposition of a project to non-technical stakeholders, such as mentors or investors.
TC: Technical Pitching Workshop- Introduce the key elements of a compelling technical pitch (e.g., problem statement, solution, market opportunity, competitive advantage).- Provide examples of successful and unsuccessful pitches.- Have students draft a 1-2 minute pitch for their project, focusing on clarity and simplicity.- Conduct a peer review session where students provide feedback on each other's pitches, with a focus on clarity and impact.

ILO: Design and deliver a roadshow presentation that effectively conveys the technical and business value of a project to a diverse audience, including non-technical stakeholders.
TC: Roadshow Presentation Design- Discuss the importance of tailoring presentations to different audiences (e.g., investors, mentors, potential partners).- Teach students how to create visually appealing and informative slides that support their pitch.- Guide students in creating a 5-7 minute roadshow presentation that includes an introduction, problem statement, solution, market analysis, and call to action.- Conduct a mock roadshow session where students present their projects to a panel of peers and instructors, followed by constructive feedback.

ILO: Refine and practice a technical pitch to ensure it is engaging, persuasive, and tailored to the specific needs and interests of non-technical stakeholders.
TC: Pitch Refinement and Practice- Review common pitfalls in technical pitching and how to avoid them (e.g., using jargon, overcomplicating the message).- Provide a checklist for evaluating the effectiveness of a pitch (e.g., clarity, engagement, relevance, call to action).- Have students refine their pitches based on previous feedback and the checklist.- Organize a final pitch session where students deliver their refined pitches to a mixed audience of technical and non-technical stakeholders, followed by a Q&A session and detailed feedback.

ILO: Demonstrate effective use of Feishu for tracking milestones, tasks, and progress
TC: Progress & PM Practice Assessment- Step 1: Feishu Workspace Walkthrough. Each group shares their Feishu project workspace (screen share) to demonstrate: 1) Milestone tracking, 2) Task assignment, 3) Progress updates (e.g., completed vs. in-progress tasks from the 2-week plan). Instructor feedback focuses on Feishu optimization.- Step 2: Progress Check. Groups report on 2-week plan achievements: 1) Completed tasks, 2) Delays (if any) + reasons, 3) Alignment with revised proposal objectives.

ILO: Apply Agile/Scrum principles (sprints, daily standups, backlog management) to structure project work and adapt to changes.
TC: Agile/Scrum Fundamentals for Project Management- Step 1: Core Concepts. Teach key Agile/Scrum principles tailored to academic projects:    a. Sprint: 2-week focused work cycle (aligns with existing 2-week plans).     b. Product Backlog: Prioritized list of project tasks (group + individual).   c. Daily Standup: 15-minute sync (via Feishu) to share "What did I do? What will I do? Blockers?".                 d. Sprint Review: End-of-sprint check-in to assess deliverables.- 2: Feishu-Scrum Integration. Demonstrate how to configure Feishu for Scrum:   a. Create a "Product Backlog" list (Feishu Tasks) with priority labels (High/Medium/Low).  b. Set up a 2-week "Sprint" board (Feishu Kanban) with columns: To Do → In Progress → Review → Done.  c. Assign task owners, deadlines, and dependencies (e.g., "Student A’s literature review must be done before Student B’s methodology setup").Groups practice configuring their Feishu workspace with these features.

ILO: Conduct a risk assessment for the current project phase, identifying potential bottlenecks and developing mitigation strategies.
TC: Early-Stage Risk Assessment & Mitigation- Step 1: Risk Identification Workshop. Guide groups to identify phase-specific risks using a "Risk Matrix" (likelihood × impact): Common risks: Resource shortages (e.g., HPC access delays), disciplinary misalignment, task dependencies causing bottlenecks, scope creep. Groups list 3–4 high-priority risks relevant to their project.- Step 2: Mitigation Strategy Development. For each high-priority risk, groups draft: 1) Preventive measures (e.g., "Secure HPC access 1 week before sprint start"), 2) Contingency plans (e.g., "If HPC is unavailable, use cloud-based alternative"), 3) Feishu tracking (e.g., "Add ‘Risk Monitor’ task with weekly check-ins").

ILO: Develop  next  2-week plan into a Scrum-style sprint plan with clear deliverables, responsibilities, and checkpoints.
TC: - Step 1: Sprint Planning Template. Introduce a Feishu-compatible "Sprint Plan Template" with sections: 1) Sprint Goal (aligned with proposal objectives), 2) Prioritized Tasks (backlog items), 3) Task Dependencies, 4) Daily Standup Schedule, 5) Sprint Review Checklist.- Step 2: Group Sprint Plan Development. Groups develop their next 2-week plan into a Scrum sprint: a. Set a clear sprint goal (e.g., "Complete prototype v1.0 design + user needs analysis"). b. Prioritize tasks (High = critical to sprint goal; Low = nice-to-have). c. Schedule daily/weekly standups (e.g., 9:30 AM via Feishu Meeting) and a sprint review (Day 14).Instructor reviews plans for feasibility and Scrum alignment.

ILO: Systematically analyze committee feedback (from group and individual Q&A) to identify gaps in Rubric 1 (Group proposal & PQA presentation rubrics) and Rubric 2 (Individual project PQA rubrics) criteria.
TC: Feedback Analysis & Gap Identification- Step 1: Group Feedback Reflection (20 mins)Teams review group presentation feedback to address Rubric-aligned gaps- Step 2: Individual Feedback Reflection (15 mins)Students work independently to map their personal feedback to Rubric criteria

ILO: Develop targeted revision plans for group and individual proposals, addressing feedback on alignment, clarity, feasibility, and academic merit.
TC: Targeted Revision Planning for Proposals- Step 1: Group Proposal Revision Plan (20 mins)Teams draft a group revision action plan, assigning owners to each gap- Step 2: Individual Proposal Revision Plan (15 mins)Students draft personal revision tasks tied to feedback

ILO: Draft a detailed project initiation plan that outlines concrete tasks, responsibilities, and milestones to launch the group and individual project components.
TC: Final Alignment & Next Steps- Teams review their revision action plans and 2-week initiation plans to confirm task ownership and deadlines.- Remind students of proposal resubmission requirements (e.g., minor revisions due in 3 days, major revisions in 7 days per PQA results).- Schedule follow-up check-in to track progress on revisions and project kickoff tasks.

ILO: Validate their drafted sections against the template’s content/formatting requirements
TC: Section Presentations & Feedback (Round 1: Core Project Overview) : Focus on Template Sections 1 (Group Project Overview) For each presenter:1. 5-Minute Section Presentation: The student walks through their drafted section, answering:- "Did I meet the template’s content requirements (e.g., Section 1.1 includes data/case examples for real-world context)?"- "How does this section align with the relevant Rubric 1 criterion (e.g., Section 1.3’s SMART objectives map to Rubric 1 Criterion 3)?"2. 3-Minute Peer Feedback: Peers use the crosswalk to flag gaps (e.g., "Section 1.3’s objectives lack measurability (template requirement) and don’t meet Rubric 1 Criterion 3’s ‘SMART’ standard").3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback: Provide example-driven revisions

ILO: Assess section alignment with Rubric 1 criteria (e.g., real-world context in Section 1.1 maps to Rubric 1 Criterion 1; group task division in Section 2.2 maps to Rubric 1 Criterion 6).
TC: Section Presentations & Feedback (Round 2: Solution, Plan & Feasibility) : Focus on Template Sections 2–4 (Integrated Solution, Implementation Plan, Feasibility/Budget) :For each presenter:1. 5-Minute Section Presentation: The student demonstrates compliance with template requirements (e.g., Section 2.1 includes a solution framework diagram; Section 3 has a milestone table; Section 4.3 uses the required budget table format) and links to Rubric 1 criteria (e.g., Section 2.1 → Rubric 1 Criterion 2 (Cross-Disciplinary Integration); Section 4.1 → Rubric 1 Criterion 4 (Feasibility)).2. 3-Minute Peer Feedback: Peers highlight gaps (e.g., "Section 2.2 doesn’t explain how disciplinary tasks interconnect (Rubric 1 Criterion 6 gap)"; "Section 4.3’s budget table is missing subtotals (template format gap)").3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback: Provide targeted fixes with examples.

ILO: Incorporate peer and instructor feedback to revise section-specific gaps
TC: Section Presentations & Feedback (Round 3: Outcomes & Formatting): Focus on Template Sections 5 (Expected Outcome) and overall formatting:1. 5-Minute Presentation: The student confirms Section 5’s outcomes align with Section 1.3’s objectives (template requirement) and validates overall formatting (page count, font, citations, figure captions per template rules). They link Section 5 to Rubric 1 Criterion 3 (Objectives & Outcomes).2. 3-Minute Peer Feedback: Peers flag gaps (e.g., "Section 5’s outcomes don’t tie to Section 1.3’s SMART objectives (Rubric 1 Criterion 3 gap)"; "Figure 1’s caption lacks sentence case (template formatting gap)").3. 2-Minute Instructor Feedback

ILO: Ensure overall proposal coherence.
TC: - Group Coherence Audit (5 mins): Teams review the full proposal draft to ensure section transitions are logical (e.g., Section 2.1’s solution addresses Section 1.2’s decomposed problem; Section 3’s milestones map to Section 1.3’s objectives).- Revision Action Plan (5 mins): Each student lists 2–3 section-specific revisions (e.g., "Add stakeholder data to Section 1.1"; "Clarify disciplinary synergy in Section 2.1") with deadlines.- Final Reminders: Reinforce submission requirements

ILO: Frame a robust real-world context and cross-disciplinary solution, clearly identifying specific societal/industry problems, stakeholders, and how integrated disciplinary knowledge adds value.
TC: Real-World Context & Cross-Disciplinary Integration- Key strategies for Rubric 1.1 (Real-World Context):1. Use data/case studies to define the problem.2. Identify 2–3 key stakeholders (beneficiaries, partners) and their needs.- Key strategies for Rubric 1.2 (Cross-Disciplinary Integration):1. Explain "disciplinary synergy" (e.g., "Computer science’s AI modeling + business’s market analysis = a tailored digitalization tool that’s both technical and user-centric").2. Avoid silos: Map each discipline’s contribution to a specific sub-problem.

ILO: Define SMART project objectives, coherent group tasks, and feasible milestones, ensuring objectives align with expected outcomes and the execution plan is resource- and time-realistic.
TC: SMART Objectives, Milestones & Feasibility- Workshop on Rubric 1.3 (Project Objectives & Outcomes):1. Teach SMART criteria with examples: Weak: "Improve digitalization" → Strong: "Develop a free AI-driven inventory tool for 50+ small businesses in Guangzhou by May 2027 (measurable, time-bound)".2. Link objectives to expected outcomes (e.g., "Objective 1 → Outcome: Prototype tested with 10 entrepreneurs; 80% report time savings").- Workshop on Rubric 1.4 (Feasibility & Milestones):1. Milestone best practices: (e.g., "Jan 2026: Complete literature review on small business digitalization gaps").2. Feasibility check: Analyze resources (expertise, budget) and risks (e.g., "Lack of business user access → Mitigation: Partner with local chambers of commerce").

ILO: Structure the proposal to meet template requirements , maintaining logical organization, avoiding component overlap, and demonstrating clear connections between individual tasks and group goals.
TC: Proposal Structure & Group Coherence- Key strategies for Rubric 1.5 (Writing Quality & Organization):1. Follow template section hierarchy (1.1 → 1.2 → 1.3) and use concise academic language.2. Avoid common pitfalls: Text-heavy tables, inconsistent formatting, or missing captions for figures/tables.- Key strategies for Rubric 1.6 (Group Coherence):1. Use Section 2.2 (Group Division & Task Alignment) to explain how individual tasks interconnect (e.g., "Student A’s AI model development → Student B’s user testing → Student C’s final tool integration").2. Eliminate overlap: Assign unique disciplinary focus to each member (e.g., "Engineering = tool development; Sociology = user needs analysis").

ILO: Iterate problem statements to be concise, action-oriented (no premature solutions) and co-develop strategic, interdisciplinary solutions that address real-world challenges.Transferable Skills: Critical Thinking (Problem Framing), Transdisciplinarity (Cross-Boundary Solution Design)
TC: Iterate Problem Statements & Develop Interdisciplinary Solutions Review Assignment 3’s problem statement requirements: concise, action-oriented, no premature solutions, plus a description of its selection/iterations.Guide the group to refine draft statements (e.g., revise “How to use apps to fix waste” to “How to reduce community waste through accessible solutions”).Co-develop 1-2 interdisciplinary solutions: Link team disciplines (e.g., “Environmental science data + business cost models to design affordable waste bins”) to address real-world needs.

ILO: Identify key stakeholders, map them by influence/interest, and articulate their (and the group’s) potential roles, motivations, and contributions to the project.Transferable Skills: Stakeholder Analysis, Teamwork (Role Alignment)
TC: Map Stakeholders & Articulate Roles Identify key stakeholders (e.g., community residents, local businesses, NGOs) using Assignment 3’s guidance.Create a shared stakeholder map (categorize by influence/interest) and detail: their roles (e.g., “Residents provide usage feedback”), motivations (e.g., “Businesses want to cut waste costs”), and the group’s role in engaging them (e.g., “We’ll survey residents to validate solutions”).

ILO: Integrate disciplinary knowledge (e.g., engineering, sociology) into individual projects, explaining how it enhances both personal work and the group’s objectives.Transferable Skills: Knowledge Synthesis, Strategic Alignment (Individual-Group Synergy)
TC: Prompt each member to list their disciplinary expertise (e.g., “I study public health—can analyze community waste habits”).Discuss how to integrate this knowledge: For example, a public health student’s data can inform the group’s solution design, while an engineering student’s prototype can support the public health student’s impact analysis.Draft 1-2 sentences per member linking their discipline to their individual project (e.g., “My public health analysis will strengthen the group’s stakeholder impact section”).

ILO: Engage in reflective practice to assess personal contributions (e.g., task completion, idea sharing) and group dynamics (e.g., communication, conflict resolution).Transferable Skills: Self-Reflection, Teamwork (Collaborative Improvement)
TC: Use a simple reflection guide: 1) “What tasks have I completed to support the group?” 2) “What challenges has the group faced (e.g., miscommunication)?” 3) “How can we improve collaboration?”Share reflections in pairs, then discuss 1-2 shared dynamics (e.g., “We need clearer task deadlines”) and agree on one action to address them (e.g., “Update the shared task tracker weekly”).

ILO: Identify gaps in the Project Brief draft by comparing with the template’s core requirements (e.g., vague problem statements, incomplete timelines).Transferable Skills: Critical thinking (gap analysis), attention to detail
TC: Template Requirements & Gap Identification Review the Project Brief template’s mandatory sections:Group Section: Title (concise), problem statement (specific), key insights (data-backed), solutions (feasible), next steps (time-bound).Individual Section: Challenge statement (aligned with group goal), skills inventory (relevant), interconnection (clear link to group work).Guide students to list common gaps in first draft(e.g., “problem statement lacks data,” “next steps missing deadlines”).

ILO: Apply revision strategies to key sections (problem statement, solutions, milestones) to enhance clarity, specificity, and alignment with group goals.Transferable Skills: Written communication, strategic alignment
TC: Revision Strategies for Key Sections Teach targeted revision methods:Problem Statement: Replace vague phrases (e.g., “a big issue”) with data (e.g., “70% of users report delays”).Solutions: Add feasibility details (e.g., “We’ll test the app with 50 users first”).Milestones: Attach specific dates (e.g., “Finish prototype by Oct 30”).Individual Interconnection: Explicitly link to group goals (e.g., “My user research will inform the group’s solution design”).

ILO: Collaboratively review peers’ sections, provide constructive feedback, and reach consensus on final revisions.Transferable Skills: Teamwork (peer feedback), interpersonal communication
TC: Peer Review & Collaborative RevisionStructure peer feedback:Pair review: Comment on 1 strength and 2 revision needs per section (e.g., “Your solution is clear, but add testing details”).Group discussion: Address conflicting feedback, prioritize revisions (e.g., “Let’s first fix the problem statement’s data gap”).

ILO: Self-assess the revised brief against the template’s criteria to ensure readiness for submission.Transferable Skills: Self-evaluation, quality control
TC: Final Self-Check Use a checklist based on the template:Group section: All fields complete? Solutions align with problem? Next steps have deadlines?Individual section: Challenge specific? Skills relevant? Interconnection clear?Log unresolved issues for final adjustments.

ILO: Collaboratively finalize the group section of the Project Brief (title, problem statement, insights, solutions, next steps) for clarity and alignment with project goals. Transferable Skill: Teamwork, Cross-Bounday Integration
TC: Completing Project Brief Template (Group + Individual Sections)TC 1: Group Section Collaboration Review Project Brief group fields:Title: Draft a concise, impactful title (e.g., “AI-Powered Waste Sorting for Communities”).Problem Statement: Refine the core challenge (e.g., “Residents struggle to sort recyclables accurately”).Key Insights: Share research findings (e.g., “70% of waste is mis-sorted due to unclear labels”).Solutions: Propose 1–3 feasible innovations (e.g., “AI-enabled sorting bins with visual guides”).Next Steps: Define 2–4 week actions (e.g., “Test AI prototype at 2 local buildings by [date]”).

ILO: Each member completes individual sections (challenge statement, skills inventory, group interconnection) to define personal contributions and alignment.Transferable Skill: Roles & Responsibility, Systematic Problem Definition
TC: Individual Section CompletionGuide members on individual fields:Challenge Statement: Focus on a sub-problem (e.g., “Develop AI image-recognition for waste types”).Skills Inventory: List relevant expertise (e.g., “Python, computer vision”).Interconnection: Explain how personal work supports the group (e.g., “AI model powers group’s sorting bins”).

ILO: Use peer feedback and template guidelines to identify gaps (e.g., vague problem statement) and plan revisions.Transferable Skill: Self/Peer Assessment for Document Quality, Interpersonal & Collaborative Communication
TC: Gap Identification & Revision Planning Self/peer-check for gaps (e.g., “Next steps lack deadline,” “Interconnection too vague”). Log revisions (e.g., “Add ‘finish AI training by [date]’ to next steps”).

ILO: Evaluate problems from the EPC Problem Bank using Session 3’s four core criteria (Real-world Relevance, Openness, Interdisciplinarity, Educational Suitability) to shortlist 2–3 viable options for the group project. Transferable Skills: Critical Evaluation (sub-skill: criterion-based problem screening)
TC: EPC Problem Bank Criteria Review & Shortlisting This module focuses on reinforcing Session 3’s problem evaluation standards and guiding teams to screen the EPC Problem Bank systematically. First, lead a recap of Session 3’s four core criteria with concrete examples. Second, guide a shortlisting activity: Each student first reviews the EPC Problem Bank independently, then the group comes together to discuss 2–3 shortlisted problems, ensuring each selection considered the four criteria.

ILO: Identify and connect with peers sharing interest in the shortlisted problems (via structured matching), then confirm team formation with clear alignment on problem focus (to support Assignment 3’s group project). Transferable Skills: Collaboration & Networking (sub-skill: interest-based team coordination)
TC: This module supports ILO 2 by facilitating structured peer connection and team confirmation. Start with an “interest pitch” session: Each student takes 1 minute to present their 2–3 shortlisted problems, highlighting why they find the problems meaningful. For in-person settings, use “interest badges”to help students visually identify peers with overlapping for virtual/hybrid settings, use a shared Google Sheet or Miro “Interest Map” to visualize matches.

ILO: Refine 1 shortlisted problem into a draft problem statement that meets Session 3’s “strong statement” standards (e.g., articulates significance, avoids over-specification, reflects interdisciplinary potential). .Transferable Skills: Problem Framing (sub-skill: structured problem statement development)
TC: Once interests are confirmed, guide teams of students to form. Each team documents three key details: team name and contact information for all members, the final problem selected (via majority vote, with the group justifying the choice using Session 3’s criteria), and an initial “interest fit” check—each member confirms they understand the problem’s core and agree to focus on it to avoid misalignment later.

ILO: Draft a 1-page “Problem-Team Alignment Plan” that links the refined problem to team roles (e.g., “stakeholder research lead”) and key milestones for Assignment 3 (e.g., “finalize proposal outline by Oct 1”). Transferable Skills: Project Coordination (sub-skill: team-task alignment for long-term assignments)
TC: This module prepares teams for Assignment 3 by linking the refined problem to actionable roles and milestones. First, guide role allocation: Assign roles that directly support the selected problem’s needs. Ensure roles reflect the problem’s interdisciplinary potential. Then, set key milestones for Assignment 3 with clear deadlines and owners. Finally, compile roles, milestones, and owners into a 1-page “Problem-Team Alignment Plan”.

ILO: Integrate Session 1’s Design Thinking (DT) framework (5 phases, RBM mapping) and Session 2’s empathy tools (Empathy Maps, 5 Whys) to refine the group’s stakeholder analysis (from Assignment 1).Transferable Skills: Systems Thinking (sub-skill: cross-session knowledge integration)
TC: Progress Alignment: Session 1/Session 2 Recap & Gap Identification- Recap Check: Quick group discussion to confirm mastery of key concepts: Session 1: DT 5 phases (Empathize→Define→Ideate→Prototype→Test), stakeholder context diagrams.Session 2: Empathy Map components (thoughts/feelings/actions/pains), 5 Whys root cause analysis.- Gap Analysis: Use a “Progress-Gap Table” to log:① Completed work (e.g., “Assignment 1 stakeholder list”).② Unfinished work blocking empathy research.

ILO: Apply Session 2’s root cause analysis techniques (5 Whys/fishbone diagram) to identify 1–2 core pain points of key stakeholders, supported by evidence (e.g., interview snippets, secondary data).Transferable Skills: Problem-Solving (sub-skill: evidence-based pain point diagnosis)
TC: Empathy & Pain Point Refinement: Tool Application - Empathy Map Optimization: Teams use Miro/Mural to update their initial stakeholder map (from Assignment 1) into a full Empathy Map:① Fill in each stakeholder’s “thoughts” (e.g., “teachers worry about time”), “feelings” (e.g., “frustrated”), “actions” (e.g., “skip training”), “pains” (e.g., “no easy access to resources”).② Apply 5 Whys to 1 top pain (e.g., “Pain: ‘teachers skip training’ → Why? ‘No time’ → Why? ‘Training is 2hrs’).

ILO: Collaboratively iterate the group’s investigation plan (from Assignment 1) to include empathy research steps (e.g., user interviews, observation) and align with Assignment 2 requirements.Transferable Skills: Project Planning (sub-skill: plan refinement for assignment alignment)
TC: Investigation Plan Iteration: Prepare for Assignment 2- Plan Refinement: Teams revise their Assignment 1 investigation plan to add Session 2-aligned steps:① Add empathy research methods (e.g., “conduct 5 teacher interviews Oct 1–5”).② Include root cause verification (e.g., “validate 5 Whys findings with 2 peers”).- Task Allocation: Use a “Role-Checkpoint Table” to assign:① Roles (e.g., “A leads interview scheduling, B analyzes interview notes”).② Checkpoints of interview questions.

ILO: Assign clear roles for executing the iterated investigation plan (e.g., “lead stakeholder interviews”) and set time-bound checkpoints to ensure progress toward Assignment 2’s due date.Transferable Skills: Team Collaboration (sub-skill: accountability and task allocation)
TC: Investigation Plan Iteration: Prepare for Assignment 2- Plan Refinement: Teams revise their Assignment 1 investigation plan to add Session 2-aligned steps:① Add empathy research methods (e.g., “conduct 5 teacher interviews Oct 1–5”).② Include root cause verification (e.g., “validate 5 Whys findings with 2 peers”).- Task Allocation: Use a “Role-Checkpoint Table” to assign:① Roles (e.g., “A leads interview scheduling, B analyzes interview notes”).② Checkpoints of interview questions.

ILO: Effectively utilize virtual collaboration platforms (e.g., Google Workspace for Education and Microsoft Teams) to facilitate seamless team communication and project management.
TC: Introduction to Virtual Collaboration Tools: - Demonstrate the key features and functionalities of Google Workspace for Education and Microsoft Teams. - Guide students through setting up a shared workspace, creating and managing documents, and using chat and video call features. - Assign a small group task where students must use these tools to collaborate on a short, focused project (e.g., a one-page summary of a recent article).

ILO: Create and manage a shared project calendar using virtual collaboration platforms to ensure all team members are aware of deadlines and milestones.
TC: Project Calendar Setup and Management: - Instruct students on how to create and share a project calendar in Google Workspace for Education or Microsoft Teams. - Teach them to set up recurring meetings, reminders, and notifications. - Have each team create a detailed project timeline with specific milestones and deadlines, and share it with the instructor and other team members. - Conduct a brief session on best practices for maintaining and updating the calendar.

ILO: Develop and implement a virtual file management system to organize and store project-related documents and resources, ensuring easy access and version control.
TC: Virtual File Management: - Explain the importance of organized file management in collaborative projects. - Show students how to create and structure folders in Google Drive or Microsoft OneDrive. - Teach them to use naming conventions, version control, and sharing permissions effectively. - Assign a task where each team creates a folder structure for their project, uploads relevant documents, and sets up sharing permissions. - Review and provide feedback on the organization and accessibility of the file systems created by each team.

ILO: Effectively use interactive whiteboards and smart displays to facilitate dynamic, digital brainstorming sessions and enhance collaborative problem-solving. Transferable Skills: Digital Collaboration, Creative Problem-Solving
TC: Interactive Whiteboards & Smart Displays for Brainstorming- Step 1: Introduction to Tools (15 mins)Demonstrate the features of interactive whiteboards and smart displays.- Step 2: Collaborative Brainstorming (30 mins)Students use the tools to brainstorm ideas for a project, adding and organizing notes in real-time.- Step 3: Reflection and Feedback (15 mins)Discuss the effectiveness of the tool and gather feedback on the brainstorming process.

ILO: Utilize digital project management tools like Trello, Asana, or Microsoft Planner to organize tasks, set deadlines, and track progress collaboratively. Transferable Skills: Project Management, Time Management, Teamwork
TC: Digital Project Management Tools- Step 1: Introduction to Tools (20 mins)Introduce and demonstrate the features of Trello, Asana, or Microsoft Planner.- Step 2: Create a Project Plan (40 mins)Students create a project plan, assigning tasks, setting deadlines, and tracking progress using the chosen tool.- Step 3: Review and Adjust (20 mins)Review the project plan as a group, make adjustments, and ensure everyone is aligned with the timeline and responsibilities.

ILO: Leverage online learning platforms with collaboration features (e.g., Schoology, Canvas, Moodle) to enhance communication, resource sharing, and project coordination. Transferable Skills: Digital Communication, Resource Management, Team Collaboration
TC: Online Learning Platforms with Collaboration Features- Step 1: Introduction to Platforms (20 mins)Introduce and demonstrate the features of Schoology, Canvas, or Moodle.- Step 2: Set Up a Collaborative Space (30 mins)Students set up a collaborative space within the platform, including discussion boards, file sharing, and task lists.- Step 3: Practice Collaboration (30 mins)Students practice using the platform to share resources, discuss project updates, and coordinate tasks. Reflect on the experience and gather feedback.

ILO: Create a digital portfolio that effectively showcases their PBL project, including key milestones, reflections, and multimedia elements. Transferable Skills: Digital Literacy, Visual Communication, and Project Documentation
TC: Introduce students to digital portfolio tools such as Seesaw or Adobe Spark. Provide a step-by-step guide on how to create a portfolio, including how to add text, images, videos, and links. Demonstrate best practices for organizing content and using visual elements to enhance the presentation.

ILO: Incorporate peer feedback to refine and improve the digital portfolio, ensuring it meets the project’s communication and documentation standards. Transferable Skills: Peer Review, Constructive Feedback, and Iterative Improvement
TC: Organize a peer review session where students share their portfolios with each other. Provide a structured feedback form that includes criteria such as clarity, organization, and visual appeal. Guide students in providing constructive feedback and help them identify areas for improvement. Encourage students to log and implement the feedback they receive.

ILO: Conduct a final self-assessment of the digital portfolio to ensure it meets all the required criteria and is ready for public sharing. Transferable Skills: Self-evaluation, Quality Control, and Presentation Readiness
TC: Provide a detailed checklist for the final self-assessment, covering all aspects of the portfolio, such as completeness of content, quality of multimedia elements, and adherence to the project’s standards. Instruct students to use the checklist to perform a thorough review of their portfolio. Have students log any unresolved issues and make final adjustments before submission. Emphasize the importance of presenting a polished and professional portfolio.

ILO: Effectively utilize online learning platforms with collaboration features to enhance project management and team communication. Transferable Skills: Digital Literacy, Team Collaboration
TC: Introduction to Online Learning Platforms & Collaboration Features Demonstrate the use of platforms like Schoology, Canvas, or Moodle for project management. Guide students in setting up project groups, sharing documents, and using discussion boards. Facilitate a hands-on session where students create a project timeline and assign tasks within the platform.

ILO: Integrate multimedia and interactive elements into online learning platforms to enhance engagement and understanding. Transferable Skills: Multimedia Integration, Engagement Techniques
TC: Enhancing Engagement with Multimedia & Interactive Elements Teach students how to embed videos, images, and interactive quizzes into their online projects. Provide a step-by-step guide on creating and uploading multimedia content. Encourage students to incorporate at least one multimedia element into their project and share it with the group for feedback.

ILO: Utilize analytics and feedback tools within online learning platforms to monitor progress and improve project outcomes. Transferable Skills: Data Analysis, Continuous Improvement
TC: Using Analytics and Feedback Tools for Project Improvement Introduce students to the analytics and feedback tools available in platforms like Schoology, Canvas, or Moodle. Show them how to track participation, engagement, and task completion. Guide students in setting up regular check-ins and feedback sessions, and teach them how to use the data to make informed decisions about project adjustments.

ILO: Demonstrate the ability to use interactive whiteboards and smart displays to facilitate dynamic, digital brainstorming sessions. Transferable Skills: Digital literacy, collaboration
TC: Introduction to Interactive Whiteboards and Smart Displays \\n- Overview of features and functionalities (e.g., touch controls, screen sharing, real-time collaboration). \\n- Hands-on practice: Setting up and using an interactive whiteboard for a brainstorming session. \\n- Group activity: Collaboratively create a mind map on a smart display, focusing on a project-related topic.

ILO: Apply advanced features of interactive whiteboards and smart displays to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of team collaborations. Transferable Skills: Advanced digital literacy, teamwork, problem-solving
TC: Advanced Features and Best Practices \\n- Introduction to advanced tools (e.g., annotation, screen capture, integration with other software). \\n- Demonstration: Using interactive whiteboards for real-time feedback and iteration. \\n- Group exercise: Design a project timeline using the interactive whiteboard, incorporating multimedia elements and annotations. \\n- Discussion: Sharing best practices and tips for maximizing the use of smart displays in collaborative settings.

ILO: Evaluate the impact of using interactive whiteboards and smart displays on the quality and outcomes of team projects. Transferable Skills: Critical thinking, evaluation, reflection
TC: Impact Assessment and Reflection \\n- Case study: Analyze a project that utilized interactive whiteboards and smart displays. \\n- Group discussion: Identify the benefits and challenges of using these tools in the project. \\n- Individual reflection: Write a short reflection on how the use of interactive whiteboards and smart displays influenced the project’s success. \\n- Presentation: Each group presents their findings and reflections to the class, followed by a Q&A session.

ILO: Design and develop an Augmented Reality (AR) or Virtual Reality (VR) experience that enhances the understanding of a complex concept or problem in the PBL project. Transferable Skill: Digital Literacy, Creative Problem Solving
TC: Introduction to AR/VR Tools & Platforms: Introduce students to AR/VR platforms such as Google Expeditions, Merge Cube, and Unity. Students will explore these tools and select one for their project. Hands-on Workshop: Students will design and develop an AR/VR experience using the selected platform. The experience should help to visualize and understand a complex concept or problem in their PBL project. Peer Review & Feedback: Students present their AR/VR experiences to peers, who provide feedback on the clarity, engagement, and effectiveness of the experience.

ILO: Integrate AR/VR experiences into the PBL project to enhance learning and engagement. Transferable Skill: Project Management, Interdisciplinary Collaboration
TC: Integration Planning: Students will identify key areas in their PBL project where AR/VR can be integrated to enhance learning and engagement. They will create a plan for integrating the AR/VR experience, including timelines and resources. Implementation: Students will implement the AR/VR experience into their PBL project, ensuring it aligns with the project's goals and objectives. Evaluation & Reflection: Students will evaluate the impact of the AR/VR integration on the overall project. They will reflect on the process and outcomes, identifying what worked well and what could be improved.

ILO: Evaluate the effectiveness of AR/VR in enhancing the PBL project and propose improvements. Transferable Skill: Critical Thinking, Continuous Improvement
TC: Evaluation Framework: Students will develop an evaluation framework to assess the effectiveness of the AR/VR experience in enhancing the PBL project. This framework should include criteria such as user engagement, learning outcomes, and ease of use. Data Collection & Analysis: Students will collect data from users (e.g., peers, instructors) who interact with the AR/VR experience. They will analyze this data to determine the effectiveness of the experience. Improvement Proposals: Based on the evaluation, students will propose and implement improvements to the AR/VR experience. They will document the changes and their rationale, and present the updated experience to the class for final feedback.

ILO: Effectively utilize virtual collaboration platforms (e.g., Google Workspace for Education, Microsoft Teams) to enhance group communication and project management. Transferable Skills: Digital Collaboration, Project Management
TC: Introduce and demonstrate the key features of Google Workspace for Education and Microsoft Teams that support seamless collaboration, such as document sharing, real-time editing, and video conferencing. Guide students through setting up a shared workspace and organizing it with folders, documents, and task lists. Assign a small group activity where students use these platforms to collaborate on a simple task, such as creating a shared document or planning a virtual meeting.

ILO: Develop and implement a structured workflow within virtual collaboration platforms to ensure efficient and transparent project progress. Transferable Skills: Workflow Design, Transparency in Communication
TC: Teach students how to create and manage a project timeline using tools like Gantt charts or Kanban boards within Google Workspace or Microsoft Teams. Instruct students on setting up regular check-ins and updates, and how to use these platforms to track progress and assign tasks. Have students practice by creating a sample project timeline and assigning tasks to team members, then conducting a mock check-in to discuss progress and any issues.

ILO: Leverage the advanced features of virtual collaboration platforms to facilitate complex problem-solving and decision-making processes. Transferable Skills: Advanced Digital Tools, Collaborative Problem Solving
TC: Demonstrate advanced features such as Google Forms for surveys, Google Sheets for data analysis, and Microsoft Whiteboard for brainstorming. Guide students through a case study where they use these tools to gather and analyze data, and then make a collaborative decision. For example, have students design a survey to collect data on a specific issue, analyze the results in a shared spreadsheet, and use a virtual whiteboard to brainstorm potential solutions and reach a consensus.

ILO: Effectively use digital project management tools (e.g., Trello, Asana, or Microsoft Planner) to organize and track project tasks, deadlines, and progress collaboratively. Transferable Skill: Digital Project Management, Collaboration
TC: Introduction to Digital Project Management Tools- Step 1: Overview of Tools. Provide an overview of Trello, Asana, and Microsoft Planner, highlighting their key features and benefits for project management.- Step 2: Setting Up the Project. Guide students through setting up a new project in one of the tools, including creating boards, lists, and cards.- Step 3: Task Assignment and Deadlines. Demonstrate how to assign tasks to team members, set deadlines, and add descriptions and attachments to each task.- Step 4: Tracking Progress. Show students how to update task statuses, add comments, and use features like checklists and labels to track progress.- Step 5: Collaborative Features. Highlight collaborative features such as notifications, comments, and shared views to ensure all team members are aligned and informed.

ILO: Develop a detailed project timeline using digital project management tools, ensuring that all tasks are clearly defined, assigned, and sequenced to meet project milestones. Transferable Skill: Time Management, Planning
TC: Creating a Detailed Project Timeline- Step 1: Identifying Key Milestones. Help students identify major project milestones and break them down into smaller, manageable tasks.- Step 2: Task Breakdown. Guide students through the process of breaking down each milestone into specific tasks, including estimated time and resources required.- Step 3: Sequencing Tasks. Teach students how to sequence tasks logically, considering dependencies and resource availability.- Step 4: Assigning Tasks. Show students how to assign tasks to team members within the project management tool, ensuring clear responsibility and accountability.- Step 5: Review and Adjust. Conduct a review session where students present their timelines, and provide feedback on sequencing, task assignments, and overall feasibility.

ILO: Utilize digital project management tools to monitor and adjust project plans in real-time, ensuring that the project stays on track and any issues are addressed promptly. Transferable Skill: Adaptability, Problem Solving
TC: Real-Time Project Monitoring and Adjustment- Step 1: Regular Check-Ins. Establish a routine for regular check-ins (e.g., weekly or bi-weekly) using the project management tool to discuss progress, challenges, and next steps.- Step 2: Updating Task Statuses. Teach students how to update task statuses, add comments, and attach relevant documents or links to keep the project board current.- Step 3: Issue Identification. Guide students on how to identify and flag potential issues or delays in the project, using features like @mentions and notifications to alert team members.- Step 4: Adjusting Plans. Show students how to make adjustments to the project plan, such as reassigning tasks, rescheduling deadlines, or adding new tasks as needed.- Step 5: Reporting and Documentation. Instruct students on how to generate reports and maintain documentation of project changes and decisions, ensuring transparency and accountability.

ILO: Collaboratively configure and customize an online learning platform (e.g., Schoology, Canvas, or Moodle) to establish group workspaces, shared resources, and communication channels for project-based learning. Transferable Skills: Digital Tool Mastery, Collaborative Infrastructure Setup
TC: Platform Setup and Configuration for Group Collaboration- Workspace Creation: Teams set up dedicated group spaces on the chosen platform (e.g., Schoology Groups, Canvas Groups, or Moodle Forums) with permissions for all members.- Resource Sharing: Upload and organize project materials (e.g., research documents, templates, schedules) in shared folders or modules.- Communication Tools: Configure discussion boards, chat features, or announcement systems to facilitate real-time and asynchronous team communication.

ILO: Utilize advanced collaboration features of online learning platforms (e.g., co-editing documents, peer review tools, or integrated feedback systems) to jointly develop and refine project deliverables. Transferable Skills: Collaborative Content Creation, Iterative Feedback Integration
TC: Leveraging Platform Features for Co-Creation and Feedback- Co-Editing Tasks: Use platform-integrated tools (e.g., Google Docs in Canvas, collaborative pages in Schoology) to draft and edit project components like reports or presentations simultaneously.- Peer Review Implementation: Set up and use built-in peer assessment modules or discussion threads for structured feedback on drafts.- Feedback Management: Track and incorporate comments using platform features (e.g., annotation tools, revision history) to iteratively improve work based on team input.

ILO: Monitor and manage group progress using analytics and tracking tools within online learning platforms (e.g., activity logs, completion dashboards, or milestone trackers) to ensure alignment with project timelines and goals. Transferable Skills: Project Monitoring, Data-Driven Collaboration Management
TC: Progress Tracking and Analytics for Group Accountability- Activity Monitoring: Review platform-generated data (e.g., Schoology analytics, Canvas SpeedGrader, or Moodle logs) to assess individual and group participation and task completion.- Milestone Tracking: Use platform tools (e.g., checklists, calendars, or gradebook features) to set and monitor deadlines for project phases.- Adjustment Strategies: Based on analytics, discuss and implement changes to workflows or schedules to address gaps and maintain project momentum.

ILO: Design and implement AR/VR-enhanced project prototypes using platforms like Google Expeditions or Merge Cube to visualize complex concepts in immersive environments. Transferable Skills: Digital literacy, spatial reasoning, technical implementation
TC: AR/VR Prototype Development for PBL Projects Introduce AR/VR tools: Google Expeditions for virtual field trips, Merge Cube for 3D object interaction. Guide students to map project concepts to AR/VR elements (e.g., environmental projects use Expeditions to explore ecosystems, engineering projects use Merge Cube for 3D model manipulation). Hands-on session: Students create simple AR/VR prototypes (e.g., design a virtual tour of a project site, build an interactive 3D model of a solution) and integrate them into their PBL presentations.

ILO: Conduct user testing and feedback collection in AR/VR simulations to evaluate project solutions' usability and effectiveness in simulated real-world scenarios.
TC: User Testing in AR/VR Simulations Set up AR/VR testing environments: Use Google Expeditions to simulate user scenarios (e.g., testing a public health intervention in a virtual community) or Merge Cube to prototype product interactions. Teach testing protocols: Define user tasks, collect feedback via surveys or observation in VR, analyze data for usability insights. Practical exercise: Students run a mini-test with peers, document findings (e.g., "80% of users navigated the VR interface easily"), and refine their projects based on feedback.

ILO: Collaboratively develop interdisciplinary AR/VR experiences that integrate multiple perspectives (e.g., combining data visualization, storytelling, and interactive design) to address complex PBL challenges. Transferable Skills: Transdisciplinarity (Cross-Boundary Design), Creative collaboration
TC: Interdisciplinary AR/VR Experience Co-creation Workshop on merging disciplines in AR/VR: For example, environmental science students use Expeditions for data-rich virtual tours, while design students add interactive elements via Merge Cube. Guide groups to brainstorm and storyboard an integrated experience (e.g., a VR simulation of a sustainable city combining engineering models, economic data, and social narratives). Implementation phase: Students use provided tools to build a collaborative prototype, with roles aligned to their expertise, and present it as part of their project deliverables.

ILO: Set up and configure a digital project management workspace in Trello, Asana, or Microsoft Planner, including creating projects, adding team members, and establishing basic workflows for task organization and collaboration.
TC: Digital Project Management Tool Setup & Configuration Workshop: 1. Tool Selection & Account Setup: Guide students through choosing a tool (Trello, Asana, or Microsoft Planner) and creating accounts/projects. 2. Workspace Configuration: Teach how to set up boards/lists (e.g., "To-Do," "In Progress," "Done"), add team members with roles, and create initial task cards. 3. Basic Workflow Establishment: Demonstrate creating tasks with titles, descriptions, assignees, and due dates; introduce labels/tags for categorization (e.g., "Design," "Research"). Instructor provides templates and reviews setups for functionality.

ILO: Use digital project management tools to create, assign, and track tasks with deadlines, ensuring collaborative progress monitoring and timely updates within a team.
TC: Task Management & Progress Tracking Workshop: 1. Task Creation & Assignment: Practice creating detailed tasks (e.g., "Conduct user interviews by Friday") with clear assignees and deadlines in Trello/Asana/Planner. 2. Progress Tracking Techniques: Teach how to move tasks across boards/lists (e.g., from "To-Do" to "In Progress"), use checklists for subtasks, and update statuses. 3. Collaborative Monitoring: Introduce features like comments for updates, @mentions for team communication, and deadline reminders. Groups simulate a 1-week project phase, with instructor feedback on tracking accuracy.

ILO: Apply digital project management tools to facilitate team collaboration through features like shared boards, real-time updates, and integration with communication platforms, enhancing coordination and transparency.
TC: Collaborative Features & Integration Workshop: 1. Shared Board Management: Demonstrate how to maintain shared project boards with permissions and real-time syncing across devices in Trello/Asana/Planner. 2. Integration with Communication Tools: Teach linking tasks to platforms like Slack or Microsoft Teams for notifications and discussions (e.g., "Post task updates to a team channel"). 3. Transparency Practices: Guide students in using activity logs, version history, and progress dashboards to monitor team contributions. Groups practice coordinating a mock project milestone, with instructor evaluation on collaboration effectiveness.

ILO: Create a structured digital portfolio that effectively showcases PBL project components using Seesaw or Adobe Spark, organizing content into clear sections (e.g., problem statement, process, outcomes). Transferable Skills: Digital literacy (multimedia tool usage), organizational skills (content structuring)
TC: Digital Portfolio Structure & Tool Basics - Introduction to Seesaw/Adobe Spark interface and core features (e.g., adding pages, embedding media). - Guide students to map portfolio sections to their PBL project: 1. Project overview (title, problem statement, goals). 2. Process documentation (timeline, key milestones, challenges). 3. Outcomes (final solutions, data/results, reflections). - Provide examples of effective layouts (e.g., using visuals for process steps, concise text for insights).

ILO: Integrate multimedia elements (e.g., images, videos, infographics) into digital portfolios to enhance storytelling and demonstrate project impact, ensuring alignment with PBL objectives and audience engagement.
TC: Multimedia Integration & Storytelling - Strategies for selecting and embedding media: 1. Use images/videos to document project stages (e.g., prototyping, testing). 2. Create infographics to visualize data or process flows. 3. Add audio/video reflections to convey personal insights. - Tips for alignment: Match media to portfolio sections (e.g., problem statement with relevant case study images, outcomes with result charts). - Discuss audience considerations (e.g., clarity for stakeholders, creativity for peers).

ILO: Apply peer and self-assessment techniques to refine digital portfolios, using feedback to improve clarity, coherence, and visual appeal, and iteratively update content based on project progress. Transferable Skill: Critical evaluation (quality assessment), adaptability (iterative improvement)
TC: Portfolio Refinement & Iterative Updates - Peer feedback guidelines: 1. Review portfolios for clarity (e.g., "Is the problem statement easy to understand?"). 2. Assess coherence (e.g., "Do sections flow logically from problem to solution?"). 3. Evaluate visual appeal (e.g., "Are media elements well-integrated?"). - Self-assessment checklist: Include items like "Portfolio reflects all PBL phases," "Media supports key messages." - Plan iterative updates: Schedule revisions after major project milestones (e.g., post-research, post-prototyping) to keep portfolio current.

ILO: Use interactive whiteboards and smart displays to transform traditional brainstorming sessions into dynamic, digital collaborations. Transferable Skills: Digital collaboration, visual communication, real-time idea synthesis
TC: Interactive Whiteboard Brainstorming Techniques Teach students to leverage digital tools for collaborative ideation: Setup: Configure interactive displays for multi-user input (e.g., touch, stylus, mobile devices). Idea Generation: Use digital sticky notes, mind-mapping tools, and drawing features to capture and organize ideas in real-time. Dynamic Collaboration: Enable simultaneous contributions from all team members, with features like color-coding for themes, drag-and-drop grouping, and live annotation. Integration: Link brainstorm outputs directly to project management platforms (e.g., Trello, Asana) for seamless workflow transition.

ILO: Apply interactive whiteboard features (e.g., templates, multimedia integration, voting tools) to structure and refine brainstorming sessions for enhanced clarity and engagement. Transferable Skills: Structured ideation, digital facilitation, consensus building
TC: Structured Brainstorming with Smart Displays Guide students in using advanced features to optimize sessions: Templates: Implement pre-designed frameworks (e.g., SWOT analysis, affinity diagrams) to organize ideas systematically. Multimedia Integration: Incorporate images, videos, and data visualizations to enrich discussions and spark creativity. Voting and Prioritization: Use built-in tools (e.g., polls, dot voting) to quickly assess and rank ideas, fostering group alignment. Session Documentation: Save and export session outputs as shareable files (e.g., PDFs, images) for ongoing reference and accountability.

ILO: Facilitate a collaborative brainstorming session using interactive whiteboards to synthesize diverse inputs into a cohesive project plan, ensuring all voices are heard and integrated. Transferable Skills: Facilitation, synthesis, inclusive collaboration
TC: Facilitation and Synthesis with Digital Tools Train students to lead effective digital brainstorming: Preparation: Set clear objectives and rules (e.g., time limits, contribution norms) using display agendas. In-Session Management: Guide discussions with features like timers, spotlight tools to highlight key points, and breakout rooms for subgroup ideation. Synthesis Techniques: Merge individual contributions into unified themes using clustering tools, and draft action items directly on the display. Feedback Loop: Conduct real-time feedback rounds (e.g., thumbs-up/down features) to iterate on ideas and finalize plans collaboratively.

ILO: Use Google Workspace for Education (e.g., Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Microsoft Teams to create and manage a shared virtual workspace for team collaboration, including setting up channels, document repositories, and communication protocols. Transferable Skills: Virtual Collaboration (sub-skill: platform setup and management for seamless teamwork)
TC: This module introduces students to virtual collaboration platforms essential for remote teamwork. First, guide platform selection: Compare Google Workspace for Education and Microsoft Teams based on features like real-time editing, file sharing, and meeting integration. Then, demonstrate workspace setup: Create a shared folder in Google Drive or a team in Microsoft Teams, organize channels or documents by project phases (e.g., research, planning, execution). Finally, establish communication protocols: Set guidelines for updates, feedback, and deadlines using platform tools like comments, @mentions, and calendar integrations.

ILO: Collaborate synchronously and asynchronously on a team project using virtual platforms (e.g., co-editing documents in Google Docs, conducting meetings in Microsoft Teams) to draft and refine deliverables like proposals or reports. Transferable Skills: Virtual Collaboration (sub-skill: real-time and delayed teamwork coordination)
TC: Progress Alignment: Platform Tools for Collaborative Work- Tool Recap: Quick group activity to practice key features: Google Workspace: Co-editing in Docs for brainstorming, using Sheets for task tracking, Slides for presentations. Microsoft Teams: Hosting video meetings with screen sharing, using chat for quick updates, integrating Planner for milestone management.- Workflow Integration: Use a 'Collaboration Workflow Chart' to map:① Synchronous tasks (e.g., 'live editing session on proposal draft').② Asynchronous tasks (e.g., 'individual research added to shared folder').

ILO: Refine team communication and project tracking by leveraging virtual platform features (e.g., version history in Google Docs, task assignments in Microsoft Teams) to ensure alignment and accountability in long-term assignments. Transferable Skills: Virtual Collaboration (sub-skill: enhanced team coordination and progress monitoring)
TC: Once platforms are set up, guide teams to optimize collaboration. Each team documents three key practices: platform usage log (e.g., 'Google Docs for draft iterations, Teams for weekly check-ins'), communication plan (via majority agreement, with justification based on project needs like deadlines or complexity), and an initial 'tool fit' check—each member confirms proficiency with selected features to avoid technical barriers later.
